title: GO WATCH IT...!!!
review:
Surrealism can appear to be ineffably bizarre, or inquisitively titillating, depending purely on the viewer's intellect. Though the realm of surrealism is highly nebulous and complex, but even a slight attempt at improvisation can sometimes go awry and open a Pandora's Box, making the task highly improbable and nigh impossible. This facet of reality may pose a handicap to the most gifted of the directors, but not to the genius of Christopher Nolan, who not only dabbles with the concept of surrealism, but also ingeniously blends it with the elements of Science Fiction in his latest wonder named Inception.

Not since the eras of Stanley Kubrick, Andrei Tarkovsky and Alfred Hitchcock has there been a more brilliant director than Christopher Nolan. He is, undoubtedly, one of THE most brilliant and gifted Hollywood filmmakers in history. Filmmakers like him come but just once in a lifetime. He has the ability to seduce our eyes, ears and most importantly, mind, and then delivers what he intends to deliver in full blast. Rarely have blockbusters have the gall to deliver such amounts imagination and intelligence at the same time. And yes, it is similar to the excellent anime film "Paprika" in the whole "invading dreams" plot, but the similarities end there as Nolan brings the film to a whole different level.

Visuals and intelligence rarely come together in movies at the same time, it's either all-visuals-no-smarts ("G.I. Joe", "Transformers") or the exact opposite ("Doubt", "Invictus"). In this film the excellently directed action sequences combined with immensely groundbreaking and jaw-dropping visual effects are combined smoothly with a heavy dose of intelligence and believability.

Although having an ensemble cast and financed by a Hollywood giant studio (Warner Bros), this film is a very personal film for Nolan, he wrote the film as well as directing it, and as you watch the film you get many glimpses of Nolan's perplexing, increasingly imaginative thoughts and dreams in the dialog that he writes and the plot that he sets up. Ideas have never felt more interesting and put to good use than in this film. This film is NOT for the popcorn muncher, rather it is a film for thinkers. Honestly I can't explain the plot for fear of spoiling the movie for you readers. Even the slightest hint will ruin the experience. The viewer will walk out of the cinema feeling dazed, confused and ultimately breathless. It's like a puzzle, both physically and mentally, and you have to pay attention throughout the film for the clues. However Nolan controls the spectacle of the film and is careful not to let it overwhelm the film's humanity, and this is where "Inception" shines. It is a very deep film that will have one thinking and asking questions for years to come. That's right, years. Incredible and colossal, difficult-procedural result of the most outstanding artistic production in all spheres of film production. A movie that will never leave your mind, demanding from you its regular revision. The movie, which you will discover with each new show for yourself in a new way. A mad, multi-level, impressive plot production, attached to the deepest actor images. Infinitely rich semantic context and visual component. All this is a combination of the greatest cinematic experience that Nolan dragged through all these years. He would never have become a director of N1 in the modern world if he were not true, loving his family by a man. And this is the most important thing. That - with what all "Begins" ...

A rare dream that survived so many years ...

title: An epic and deeply engrossing story
review:
'Inception' has only been around for 10 years, and yet it's already considered a classic by some movie fans. Should it be? In my opinion, definitely. Christopher Nolan is known for his movies that have a great story action-wise, and at the same time manage to hit us on a more spiritual level, and play some tricks on our minds. I think 'Inception' is his finest one, and that every person interested in modern cinema should watch it.

The dream world has been shown in quite a lot of movies, but Nolan takes it to the next level. Our main characters are what we could call "dream spies" - professionals who steal valuable information from the target's subconsciousness. Taking information from someone's brain is relatively easy, but the actual plot starts when they are asked to perform the impossible - plant an idea in the target's brain. The main characters, portrayed by Hollywood's brightest stars, fulfill all of our expectations - we root for them to succeed, and hold our breaths as their deepest secrets slowly unfold.

While most of the movie's action takes place in the dream world, there are also scenes that happen in the regular world - or do they? We can never be sure what's real and what's someone's imagination. The dreams can be composed of a number of levels, and so is the story that amazes us with its layers. Nolan's directorial genius is clearly visible there, because contrary to popular belief, it's not that easy to fool the audience. Another thing that I love is one that annoys some people - an open ending. It's a simple scene, but it allows many possible explanations. It's not necessary to explain everything in your movie, and if it doesn't create any plot holes it's a great way to add some flavor to the end result.

title: Lose yourself in Chris Nolan's dream-world. You may never want to wake up.
review:
Watching Inception was like gulping down an ice cold beer knowing the rest of the six-pack is still to go, after being lost without hope in the Gobi Desert of Hollywood re-makes, sequels and movies-by-numbers for what feels like a living eternity.

The well-crafted and all-encompassing veil of secrecy this film has been hidden under since it's, um, inception, has been catnip to Nolan fans everywhere. Inception is the most talked about non-vampire movie of the year so far and barrelled straight to number 3 on the IMDbTop 250 Films. Only The Godfather and perennial fan-boy favourite The Shawshank Redemption are more popular.

So what's all the fuss about?

I'm not telling you anything you shouldn't already know about Inception when I say this is a movie about dreams.

It's about a thief called Cobb, played by Leonardo DiCaprio (What's Eating Gilbert Grape, The Aviator), who can access people's dreams, and steal their ideas.

He has some issues to sort, and a past to atone for. One last job and he might just get the chance to go home.

Effectively, you could call Inception a heist movie. You could call it a love story. You could call it science fiction, I guess, but of this world. We all dream, imagine if those dreams weren't just ours alone.

It's immersive and thought-provoking, set in a big screen world delivered so flawlessly through seamless CGI and live action, that it feels like a film CGI was invented for.

The cast is top-notch. DiCaprio delivers, as does Marion Cotillard (La Vie en Rose, Public Enemies). Brit Tom Hardy moves from his Handsome Bob outing in RocknRolla and slots in nicely here, Joseph Gordon-Levitt (500 Days of Summer, Brick) and Ellen Page (Juno, Hard Candy) are similarly well-cast. Nolan regular Cillian Murphy (Batman Begins, The Dark Knight) is a Nolan regular for a reason, I loved him again here.

review:
Let's create a multi-leveled dream where we can extract ideas off our enemies or implant an idea bypassing memories and consciousness: groundbreaking, original, complex, cerebral, psychological, systemic, and astute. The descriptors are insufficient to bring justice to this tremendously brilliant endeavor. The dialogue also presents obscure ideas that have rarely been explored in movies, or at least that I have not seen. At the onset the mystical dialogue attempts to explain the nature of the extraction, and, as the scenes take place, the viewer gets tempted by the explanation of worlds created by an architect where subjects can get robbed from their ideas or implanted in the case of the major heist of the movie.

Simply following and understanding the complex setting and the intricacies of the implanting is a challenge. The movie navigates a fast pace and is able to explain the complex events of the movie in a surprisingly effective style. Christopher Nolan presents the essential details in snippets of interactions that bring a lively and charismatic depiction to the process of learning about the heist. We also enjoy a diverse cast that amalgamates to deliver us an interesting exploration of Cobb's (Leonardo Dicaprio) perception. Ariadne (Ellen Page) is presented as a gifted college student that is extraordinarily apt at building mazes. She progressively gets to know more about the heist and Cobb's projections manifested in her mazes and, despite her repeatedly expressing her concern; we can't help but feel her emotions of compassion, sadness, and empathy. If Cobb was to show her the depths of his unconscious, the cast needed a sensitive rendition like the one displayed by Ariadne. Arthur is also, from the first scenes, supporting Cobb despite knowing all the baggage and the risks he implicates. Even despite Arthur risking everyone's life, the group still continues with the mission and finishes in dramatic fashion.

There are so many levels at which inception can be analyzed, but what is at the pinnacle of the experience for me is the innovation and dialogue. Movies as innovative and cerebral like inception should be celebrated and rewarded for their brilliant effort.

Dom Cobb(Di Caprio) is an extractor who is paid to invade the dreams of various business tycoons and steal their top secret ideas. title: Inception - Movie Review
review:
The last time I watched Inception was nine years ago, and I didn't really like it. I thought it was way too confusing for my teenage brain, and that made it very boring to watch. Perhaps I should have watched it again before now though, because I have spent almost a decade being looked at in awe when I have told people that I don't like Inception. However, as of today, I am happy to say that I like the film quite a lot.

I don't think it's a masterpiece like some other people do, and there are still quite a few of Christopher Nolan's films that I would watch instead of this one, but it was thoroughly entertaining and I enjoyed all the storylines. It was fun to try and work out exactly what was happening, because it wasn't always clear.

All of the cast members are great in the film, but some of the highlights are Leonardo DiCaprio, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Tom Hardy, Ellen Page, and Cillian Murphy. The dynamic between all of them was fun to watch, and most of their characters were fleshed out nicely. This is especially the case for DiCaprio's character, and I was deeply moved by learning about how his past was influencing his motivations in the present. The action is mesmerising, and the whole third act is completely bonkers in all the right ways.

Unfortunately, I still find the story quite convoluted in parts, and a few decisions didn't make much sense to me. I have a feeling my score could increase on another rewatch, but I can't get it any higher just yet because of this one significant negative.

However, considering that I didn't like this film up until a few hours ago, I will consider this rewatch a massive win.

SCORE: 80%

title: Inception
review:
I'm nearly at a loss for words. Just when you thought Christopher Nolan couldn't follow up to "The Dark Knight", he does it again, delivering another masterpiece, one with so much power and rich themes that has been lost from the box office for several years. Questioning illusions vs reality usually makes the film weird, but Nolan grips your attention like an iron claw that you just can't help watching and wondering what will happen next. That is a real powerful skill a director has. No wonder Warner Bros. put their trust in him, he is THAT good of a director, and over-hyping a Christopher Nolan film, no matter what the film is about, is always an understatement instead of an overestimate like MANY films before.

Not since the eras of Stanley Kubrick, Andrei Tarkovsky and Alfred Hitchcock has there been a more brilliant director than Christopher Nolan. He is, undoubtedly, one of THE most brilliant and gifted Hollywood filmmakers in history. Filmmakers like him come but just once in a lifetime. He has the ability to seduce our eyes, ears and most importantly, mind, and then delivers what he intends to deliver in full blast. Rarely have blockbusters have the gall to deliver such amounts imagination and intelligence at the same time. And yes, it is similar to the excellent anime film "Paprika" in the whole "invading dreams" plot, but the similarities end there as Nolan brings the film to a whole different level.

Visuals and intelligence rarely come together in movies at the same time, it's either all-visuals-no-smarts ("G.I. Joe", "Transformers") or the exact opposite ("Doubt", "Invictus"). In this film the excellently directed action sequences combined with immensely groundbreaking and jaw-dropping visual effects are combined smoothly with a heavy dose of intelligence and believability.

Although having an ensemble cast and financed by a Hollywood giant studio (Warner Bros), this film is a very personal film for Nolan, he wrote the film as well as directing it, and as you watch the film you get many glimpses of Nolan's perplexing, increasingly imaginative thoughts and dreams in the dialog that he writes and the plot that he sets up. Ideas have never felt more interesting and put to good use than in this film. This film is NOT for the popcorn muncher, rather it is a film for thinkers. Honestly I can't explain the plot for fear of spoiling the movie for you readers. Even the slightest hint will ruin the experience. The viewer will walk out of the cinema feeling dazed, confused and ultimately breathless. It's like a puzzle, both physically and mentally, and you have to pay attention throughout the film for the clues. However Nolan controls the spectacle of the film and is careful not to let it overwhelm the film's humanity, and this is where "Inception" shines. It is a very deep film that will have one thinking and asking questions for years to come. That's right, years.

Once the film ends, you'll want to watch it again, for there's something new every time. This is a film that requires multiple viewing for someone to truly comprehend the film's ambiguous themes, and will be discussed by many in the future. This is an original film, no adaptation, no sequel/prequel, no remake/reboot, which is extremely refreshing having gone nearly three years of mostly unremarkable visual effects roadshows ("Avatar" be damned).

Of course, a film is not complete without the actors. Leo DiCaprio delivers an Oscar worthy performance, similar but better than his previous effort "Shutter Island". He shows glimpses of a flawed, grim, fragile man, who has knowledge about everything else but yet can't seem to come in grips with himself and his demons. Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Ellen Page, Tom Hardy, Ken Watanabe, Dileep Rao, Cillian Murphy, Tom Berenger, Michael Caine, Marion Cottilard, Pete Postlethwaite, Lukas Haas... Nolan really brings out the best in this unusual yet extremely talented group of supporting actors who make their roles their own.

title: A visual and psychological buffet
review:
A story so esoteric and complex will always leave itself open for those looking for plot holes and inconsistencies. I've read many a negative review describing these things that are, admittedly, not without merit. The naysayers have lots of good points, but I'll also argue that, considering them as I watch I this movie for the umpteenth time, for every point that removes a brick, I can easily come up with a counterpoint that replaces it (and this is one of those truly rare films that shows you something new with each viewing, making you discard one thing for another and then switch it back again).

In my humble opinion, Inception earns the hard won award for the most original and thought-provoking film I may ever see, topping even The Matrix in its ambition. I have yet to revisit this masterpiece and not consider at least one aspect or idea I may or may not have missed the previous time. Much like my own most enjoyable recurring dreams, it seems to mutate subtly to feel ephemeral and, at the same time, everlasting in its impact. I struggle to think of how anybody could have thought of something that seems as fantastical, bombastic and so rooted in what I can consider possible. It's like a philosophical epiphany. Or the most magnificent drug-induced trip.

I'll admit, it is difficult to fully relate to the characters as the dialogue almost exclusively revolves around explaining the intricacies of the physics and logistics of being a dreamworld mercenary and, as long as it's runtime ends up being, it hurries from one development to the next, forcing you to keep up or fall behind. Such is the drawback of making something of this magnitude. Then again, you never remember the minute details of a dream, only how you felt and what you were trying to seek out. And that is exactly what Di Caprio's character is trying to accomplish. The special effects do a wonderful job of distracting from this nagging feeling, as well as another pitch perfect score from Hans Zimmer.

Movies are essentially an escape, at least for me because that's what I crave. This is the closest to a waking dream I've ever been.

title: Nolan Is An Architect
review: Nolan helms and pens a sublime science fiction thriller. This film has outstanding direction, cinematography, screenplay, settings, score and acting. The score plays just as an important role as the characters as it creates a thrilling and intense tone to the film. All of the artists involved deliver superlative performances. In particular Page, Gordon-Levity, Murphy, Hardy, Watanabe, Cotillard and Caine are superb. However it is DiCaprio who commands the screen. The plot is so complex, but I'll try to sum it up concisely keeping in mind I'll be leaving out intricate details. A powerful Japanese business man Saito wants an idea planted in the mind of the heir, Robert, to his competitor's energy conglomerate so that Robert will dissolve the company when he takes over control. Saito bribes Cobb who is an extractor to do the job. Typically an extractor is part of a team that performs corporate espionage by infiltrating the subconscious through a shared dream world and then stealing valuable information. Basically they are thieves for hire. Cobb has a criminal past which prevents him from entering the U.S. to see his children which Saito can fix with his powerful influence, so Cobb accepts the job. Cobb and his partner Arthur enlist the help of a conman Eames, a chemist Yusef who creates a sedative to create a stable dreamworld and Ariande who is an architect that builds the puzzle of the dream's landscape. In order to wake up from a dream a member from the team must stay behind at each level to set up a kick which awakens the remaining sleeping members. If a dreamer does not wake up from the kick they are stuck in Limbo which is nearly impossible to escape from and the dreamer doesn't even realize they are still in a dream. A dreamer has an object called a totem which distinguishes the dream world from reality. Cobb and his team are going to try to do what has never been done before successfully. Plant an idea in Robert's mind during a 10 hour flight which requires planting an idea by invading a dream within a dream within a dream. This will also require a simultaneous kick to awaken the team members from the multi-level dream at the same time. Cobb reveals that he and his wife Mal had been stuck in Limbo when first experimenting with dream technology and built a world which she refused to leave and come back to reality. She is stuck in Cobb's mind as a projection. The team is pulling off the mission with Mal attempting to subterfuge it at every angle. Saito ends up getting injured and death in a dream results in Limbo. The team members all awake from the simultaneous kick except for Cobb who stays behind to find an aged Saito. He uses his totem to remind Saito of their agreement. The plot is intense, thrilling, mind-blowing, intelligent, duplicitous, ingenious, cathartic and has an ambiguous ending. I had to watch this mind- bending labyrinth film a few times to truly understand and appreciate it's brilliance. In this viewer's opinion it is Nolan's masterpiece and is at the very top if not the best film in it's genre.

title: IT IS NOT COMPLICATED AS THE DREAM GOES!
review: Her Nolan always thinks uniquely in the making of superheroes, psychological, thriller and science fiction movies. His uniqueness of screenplay and storytelling has its best on Inception. Maybe first time watchers have to see it again to understand but as a movie follower I really enjoyed every piece of the movie making.

'Inception', is one of the best overrated films ever.

It is one of my mates favourite films. A couple of years ago, we were chatting and he mentioned 'Inception' naming it as his 4th favourite film ever (his top three being all three 'Lord of the Rings' films). I wasted no time. I was straight down to HMV, picked up a copy, caught the bus home and threw it into the machine...

I liked it. I didn't have a lot of complaints about it. But the one thing I never have, was loved 'Inception'. The next day, I went back into school and told him my opinion... I said "I don't think it's one of the best films ever made".

And then he said... "you didn't understand it, did you?"

Nope. That's not what happened. I understood it perfectly. I heard Chinese whispers that it was a film you benefit from on the rewatch, so that night, I gave it another go. I enjoyed it exactly the same as before, not learning anything new about the narrative. My opinion was unchanged.

There are some popular films that I don't love. I have never really been a fan of 'Leon: The Professional', but I have never been quite able to put my finger on why. With 'Inception', I knew immediately why I didn't love it... the characters.

'Inception' is currently lurking around the number #10 spot on IMDb's top 250. If you look at the films above it, you'll notice something. 'The Shawshank Redemption' is a tale of well... redemption and what it means to be free. 'The Godfather' is a tale of a young man who slowly becomes a ruthless gang lord for the meaning of family. Even Christopher Nolan's previous effort 'The Dark Knight' has a legitimate claim to a place on the list, taking apart the tortured mind of a campy superhero, the toll his lifestyle takes on him and the effect it has on the city around him.

'Inception' is a well made film, visually it's stunning... and the concept just about works. I particularly like the fact that Nolan used special effects whenever absolutely necessary, using practical effects that lazy filmmakers would otherwise avoid. But for a film to be a masterpiece, a true masterpiece, it also has to present us with characters that go on a journey.

Now, I know what you're thinking. "This guy clearly hasn't seen the film. Dom Cobb is a brilliant character! He went on a journey! He is a tortured mind! His backstory is tragic!".

There are ideas, and then there's execution. I can see where Nolan was trying to go with the character of Cobb, and I can see what fans of 'Inception' see within the character of Cobb. But I would still argue that the character doesn't go anywhere. Sure, he gets a chance to see his kids at the end... but that's not a journey. That's a moment within a journey. Cobb kept saying "if we get this job, I will get the chance to see my kids again" and yet I have never understood why. I have seen the film about six or seven times now and I still don't know why this is the case, Nolan's writing didn't show us why, it just told us.

The thing is, that Cobb is one of the most interesting characters in the whole film. Joseph Gordon-Levitt's 'Arthur' is perhaps the weakest of the ensemble (even though he is the focus of the films most thrilling sequence), his character is literally just there for exposition. Practically every line he says in the film is describing what's going on. And then there's Ellen Page, she goes nowhere to.

Tom Hardy was quite fun though. Sure, there's still no development, but he did give the film it's much needed shot of wit. However, I would argue that the best aspect of this film, comes from the most underapreciated actor of our generation... Cillian Murphy. Both the writing and performance of his character actually give this film its backbone, it's just a shame that Nolan keeps pushing him to the sidelines, instead wishing to focus more on the uninteresting concept of the film itself.

Don't get me wrong, I liked the concept of the film. The execution is never terrible, it's just missing a little something. As of recently, however, I think I have identified how this film can be improved... by not making it a film at all. It should have been a TV show.

Hear me out! I have two main complaints about this film... 1) The characters don't have enough to do, they are merely puppets to drive the special effects forward; 2) The first half of this film is just a lazy exposition dump.

Both of these problems can be rectified with a slow burn narrative. A TV show would have given us more time with the characters. The revelations of Cobb's past could have been spread over a season rather than awkwardly crammed near to one another. It also would have given us more time with the supporting cast, perhaps given Arthur a little backstory would have saved him from being an exposition machine and Tom Hardy could have been that Spike-esque character who was every bodies favourite.

The format would also soften the blow of the exposition dumb. There is a solid half hour-forty minutes of this film, just explaining the rules of entering dreams. This was a necessary decision within a two and a half hour film, but it just constantly feels like you're being whacked in the face by a fish for 30 minutes. Nolan was like "dreams do this... they also do this... and this... and this... and this...". I'm 17 years old Chris! I don't need to be spoon fed the rules any more, the rules should have been disguised within the narrative.

Of course, if 'Inception' did follow the TV show format we probably wouldn't have got DiCaprio, Tom Hardy or Michael Caine involved. The special effects probably would have been less impressive to, and Hans Zimmer's sensational score would have been noticeably absent to. The problem is that these were the best aspects of the film. So for the characters to be great, you're gonna have to sacrifice everything that made the film good in the first place. Which is probably not an option.

Nevertheless, I would argue that Nolan made the best possible film he could have made with the concept that he had. It's a film that I would recommend everyone experience at least once because visually is just so damn impressive. And if you love this film, if it's one of your favourite films ever, I won't argue with you. But in my eyes, it's not a masterpiece. That word is sacred and should only be awarded to films that do something sensational and change the lives of everyone that watches it.

I understand the narrative of 'Inception' perfectly, and I understand why the modern generation rates it so highly... I just don't agree with the reasons why the modern generation rate it so highly. [16/20]

title: Great
review:
Leonardo DiCaprio stars as Dom Cobb, a specialist in the practice of 'extraction,' the vaguely criminal art of entering the dreams of a subject -- or of luring a subject into dreamscapes built to deceive -- and stealing secrets from his or her subconscious. Cobb practices his craft in the employ of corporations and governments and always on the lam; he's unable to return to his family in America because he's the prime suspect in a mysterious death.

A chance to exonerate himself and return home is offered him by a client (Ken Watanabe) who wants something far more difficult than simple extraction; he wants Cobb and his team to perform an 'inception' -- to plant an idea in a subject so that he embraces it as his own. But there's a problem: The target, industrial heir Robert Fischer Jr. (Cillian Murphy) has been trained in fighting off extractors; breaking into his innermost mind will thus be a physical fight (or, rather, a virtual physical fight) as much as a logical one.

It's not a job that Cobb can pull off alone. He has his perennial right-hand man, the sharp and crafty Arthur (Joseph Gordon-Levitt), aboard. He calls on an old colleague, the shady forger Eames (Tom Hardy). And he enlists new allies, a master of sleeping potions (Dileep Rao) and a brilliant puzzle-maker and instinctive mind-explorer named Ariadne (Ellen Page) who's given the job to build not one, not two but three labyrinthine dreamscapes through which Cobb can lead Fischer to an unguarded place where the inception can occur.

Sound tricky? Well, it's just the start: As Ariadne discovers, to her fear and horror, Cobb can't descend too deep into a dreamworld without encountering Mal (Marion Cotillard), his beloved wife and fellow extractor and the person whom he is suspected of killing. Diving into a target's subconscious brings Cobb perilously close to the most volatile and dangerous parts of his own. And as an inception requires him to go to profound depths, he can't bring it off without exposing himself to the thing that most terrifies and beguiles him in all the world.

So you've got an action picture with truly stupendous sequences in sometimes mind-bending settings, you've got an intellectual thriller in which achieving the goal means risking one's own sanity, and you've got a logical puzzle which, at some moments, is simultaneously five or more layers deep. (You've also got a nifty extended metaphor for the filmmaking process, with Cobb standing in for Nolan at the center of a creative group that's trying to trick people into thinking that their waking dreams are actual reality, but I'm saving that discussion for my Ph.D. thesis....)

title: A true classic of its genre
review: The major problem with sci-fi movies, especially with space and alien themed ones is that they're laden with so many logic defying crapshoot that it's difficult to sit through them with an adult brain. This is one of the reasons why I disliked and rated Interstellar poorly. Where Interstellar fails, however, Inception excels as a stark contrast to Nolan's latter project. The only nonsense you need to swallow is that people can communicate and collaborate in their dreams. Indeed, there are so many crackpots who claim more outrageous things than dream collaboration that this plot may even sound plausible to some. Once you can see beyond it you discover a very well-crafted story which runs multiple layers deep and keeps you wondering what comes next. When I was going to watch it for the first time, my friends (who had already seen it) challenged me to try to understand the movie on my first viewing. I immediately accepted the challenge. I started with a goal to accomplish what the movie meant, and largely accomplished that goal. I say largely, because the very beginning of the movie confused me and it took me a few rewinds to understand what was going on.

The cast was great, the story unique. A thief who runs a racket of sneaking into people's dreams and stealing ideas and secrets is hired by a rich dude who wants the former to enter into a business rival's head. Only this time, he has to 'plant' an idea, not steal, which has never been done before. What follows next is a typical hiring process of accomplices reminiscent of heist movies like Ocean's Eleven along with complex planning and almost flawless execution.

Mr. Nolan is known for his non-linear story-lines, and this one is no different. The story is relaxed, but requires too much thinking on the viewer's part to grasp what the heck is going on. If you are one of those who leave your brains back at home while watching a movie, believing to just 'go with the flow', then this movie is not for you. It requires utmost attention, grasping every dialogue. It's like solving a math problem. You cannot reach the next step unless you understand the current one.

Having said that, I would say I immensely enjoyed the movie, and it was a truly unique story-line unlike any other movie I have ever seen. As a sci-fi fan, I liked this movie a lot, and it ranks right up with the greatest movies of all time.

title: a masterpiece
review:
Just when you thought Christopher Nolan couldn't follow up to "The Dark Knight", he does it again, delivering another masterpiece, one with so much power and rich themes that has been lost from the box office for several years. Questioning illusions vs reality usually makes the film weird, but Nolan grips your attention like an iron claw that you just can't help watching and wondering what will happen next. That is a real powerful skill a director has. No wonder Warner Bros. put their trust in him, he is THAT good of a director, and over-hyping a Christopher Nolan film, no matter what the film is about, is always an understatement instead of an overestimate like MANY films before.

Not since the eras of Stanley Kubrick, Andrei Tarkovsky and Alfred Hitchcock has there been a more brilliant director than Christopher Nolan. He is, undoubtedly, one of THE most brilliant and gifted Hollywood filmmakers in history. Filmmakers like him come but just once in a lifetime. He has the ability to seduce our eyes, ears and most importantly, mind, and then delivers what he intends to deliver in full blast. Rarely have blockbusters have the gall to deliver such amounts imagination and intelligence at the same time. And yes, it is similar to the excellent anime film "Paprika" in the whole "invading dreams" plot, but the similarities end there as Nolan brings the film to a whole different level.

Visuals and intelligence rarely come together in movies at the same time, it's either all-visuals-no-smarts ("G.I. Joe", "Transformers") or the exact opposite ("Doubt", "Invictus"). In this film the excellently directed action sequences combined with immensely groundbreaking and jaw-dropping visual effects are combined smoothly with a heavy dose of intelligence and believability.

The cinematography is absolutely, beautifully shot, so we can see the action and emotion in all their glory. Production design is top notch, with terrific design of sets and locations. Hans Zimmer's complementing music score is simply outstanding, and knowing the man, that's really all I have to say. Together all of these elements combine to deliver a mesmerizing movie experience like no other this year.

Christopher Nolan has once again outdone himself. He truly is a gifted filmmaker, arguably the most imaginative in Hollywood today. And "Inception" can proudly stand alongside "Blade Runner" and "2001: A Space Odyssey" as science-fiction masterpieces that push the boundaries for movie making and become a different experience altogether.

There are two types of films: the crowd-pleasing blockbuster and the intelligent indie/art film. Nolan has combined two of these tropes together into one exceptionally brilliant package, pulling off that rare, now nearly-extinct Movie Magic that has since been wiped off the planet by sequelitis and reboots. Movie of Summer 2010? Movie of 2010? Heck this is possibly the first masterpiece of the decade! Nolan is a genius and I applaud him for treating his audiences as intelligent people.

Surrealism can appear to be ineffably bizarre, or inquisitively titillating, depending purely on the viewer's intellect. Though the realm of surrealism is highly nebulous and complex, but even a slight attempt at improvisation can sometimes go awry and open a Pandora's Box, making the task highly improbable and nigh impossible. This facet of reality may pose a handicap to the most gifted of the directors, but not to the genius of Christopher Nolan, who not only dabbles with the concept of surrealism, but also ingeniously blends it with the elements of Science Fiction in his latest wonder named Inception. Nolan created a niche for himself a decade back by unleashing a monster of a movie called Memento. He further substantiated his status by conjuring movies like Insomnia, The Prestige, Batman Begins, and The Dark Knight. His unremitting desire for innovation and uncanny craving to foray into the unexplored realms of imagination deservedly earned him an auteur tag, which gave him the carte blanche that a story-teller like Nolan desperately needs. It's highly apparent that Nolan takes every possible advantage of this liberty while filming Inception. Inception is not only dreamlike, but is a dream in itself and is superior to any other thing conceived on the silver screen. With its entwined layers, the movie for the most part serves as an unfathomable riddle and makes multiple viewing extremely essential. It incredibly does extremely well on both the humanistic as well as the technical fronts. In fact, the balance between human emotions and the elements of Science Fiction is so adequate that it's impossible to separate them.

The movie is about a futuristic world where the human mind can be intercepted through dream invasion. Cobb is an expert in the art of extracting information (stealing valuable secrets) from deep within the subconscious in the dream state. His proficiency in extraction is marred by a turmoil that begins with his wife's untimely death. He is forced to live the life of a fugitive away from his children. His only chance for redemption lies with a Japanese tycoon named Saitu, who wants him to do an inception (planting information into someone's mind). In order to accomplish this unprecedented task, Cobb and his team must overcome a labyrinth of unforeseeable challenges, where even a slight miss could trap them in a perpetual limbo. Leonardo Dicaprio gives a solid performance in the lead role, following his memorable performance in Shutter Island. He has brilliantly depicted the complexities and limitations of Cobb's enigmatic character highlighting his pain and mental trauma. Marion Cotillard is ravishingly scintillating as Cobb's whimsical wife, Mal. The rest of the cast has given a thorough performance with special mention of Ken Watanabe, Ellen Page and Joseph Gordon-Levitt.

Inception is incredibly brilliant as a movie and is a breakthrough in contemporary cinema. Nolan's creativity and his unparalleled execution definitely make it an object of great cachet, but whether it would become BuÃ±uel's 'Un chien andalou' or Kubrick's '2001: A Space Odyssey' and serve as a prototype for the movies to come is for the time to decide. title: The Depth of a simple story
review:
This is the one specific movie that made me fall in love in filmmaking. Nolan movies are known for a fresh feeling for your brain. Not only because he gives a new perspective to a simple theme, but because of his precise non-linear storytelling.

One of the inspirations for this movie is the method "lucid dreaming", which is a gigantic world to explore itself. But while that is a mentally achieved state, in Inception the clarity is achieved through military technology, too. This leads to more possibility.

People call this movie: complicated. But a complicated movie doesn't satisfy your mind. It's more like Nolan finds the depth in a simple theme. We explore a big world in something small.

Throughout the movie we emotionally learn more about Cobb, played by Leo. I think his performance was very underrated. I can't think of any other character to be Cobb.

Not only an inspiring, but emotional score is delivered by Hans Zimmer. This is one the best background scores ever. It fits perfectly to every second of the movie.

This movie is totally not for: 1) people who want to know everything about a character. 2) people who try to find a mistake in character's decisions. Actually those people can't watch any movie or even live their own life. We people don't take the easiest path. We take the path we individually feel the most comfortable. If you pay attention to Cobb's mental status, you would find the answer yourself why he didn't take the "easy" paths and this bigger road felt safer to him.

title: The perfect movie.
review:
Reviewing Inception is the most positive reason I can think of to reflect upon what makes movies such a special part of our lives. Is it a perfect movie? NO! Is it THE Perfect movie? Yes! Going to the movies is an exploration of fantasy, and the limits of imagination. With that comes everything that makes being a human being beautiful. Most people will experience tragedy in their life, elation, triumph, and failure. Conveying these experiences into relatable emotions is a nearly impossible task. Watching the movie Inception will bring you into a sense of the only things that are of any 'REAL VALUE' in any (and everyone's) lifespan. Love, Integrity, Hope, Purpose, and Memory after we're gone.

Spoilers are not needed, but watching Inception more than once is likely required. It is a beautiful masterpiece showcased with breathtaking visuals, tear-jerking acting, and a meaningful plot that transcends religion as well as culture.

It is a beautiful movie beyond description that can only be cheapened by explanation. Never confuse the truly important moments in life as expendable. The most special moments are fleeting, and in reality, there is no device that can allow a person to get closure for things that we have allowed to pass us by.

If it takes a powerful movie to remind us of these truths, then I suggest you watch Inception now.

The world premiere of the movie, directed by Hollywood's most inventive dreamers, was shown in London and has already got top notch reviews worldwide and has scored maximum points! Now the question arises what the movie has that it deserve all this?

Dom Cobb(Di Caprio) is an extractor who is paid to invade the dreams of various business tycoons and steal their top secret ideas. Cobb robs forcefully the psyche with practiced skill, though he's increasingly haunted by the memory of his late wife, Mal (Marion Cotillard), who has a nasty habit of showing up in his subconscious and wreaking havoc on his missions. Cobb had been involved so much in his heist work that he had lost his love!

But then, as fate had decided, a wealthy business man Saito( Ken Watanabe) hands over the responsibility of dissolving the empire of his business rival Robert Fischer Jr.(Cillian Murphy). But this time his job was not to steal the idea but to plant a new one: 'Inception'

Then what happens is the classic heist movie tradition. To carry out the the task, Cobb's 'brainiac' specialists team up again with him, Arthur (Joseph Gordon-Levitt), his longtime organizer; Tom Hardy (Eames), a "forger" who can shapeshift at will; and Yusuf (Dileep Rao), a powerful sedative supplier.

There is only one word to describe the cinematography, the set designs and the special effects, and that is Exceptional! You don't just watch the scenes happening, you feel them. The movie is a real thrill ride. The action scenes are well picturised and the music by Hans Zimmer is electronically haunting. Never, in the runtime of the movie, you will get a chance to move your eyes from the screen to any other object.

Leonardo, who is still popularly known for Jack Dawson played by him in Titanic, should be relieved as his role as Dom Cobb will be remembered forever. His performance may or may not fetch him an Oscar but it will be his finest performance till date. The supporting cast too did an extraordinary work. Christopher Nolan, ah! what a man he is. His work is nothing less than a masterpiece and he deserves all the awards in the 'Best Director' category. If "Inception" is a metaphysical puzzle, it's also a metaphorical one: It's hard not to draw connections between Cobb's dream-weaving and Nolan's film making, intended to seduce us, mess with our heads and leave an ever-lasting impression.

To conclude, I would just say before your life ends, do yourself a favor by experiencing this exceptionally lucid classic created by Nolan!

My Rating: 10/10

title: Inception
review:
Inception is written, produced, and directed by Christopher Nolan. The film stars Leonardo DiCaprio, Ken Watanabe, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Marion Cotillard, Ellen Page, Tom Hardy, Cillian Murphy, Dileep Rao, Tom Berenger, and Michael Caine. The musical score is by Hans Zimmer and Wally Pfister is the cinematographer. Plot finds DiCaprio playing Dom Cobb, a specialised spy for hire who steals ideas from the dreams of people. But one day he gets a different offer, one that will enable him to see his estranged children. To get his reward he must enact Inception, the planting of an idea in the mind of the selected target. But Inception is thought impossible and should Cobb and his selected team fail? The consequences are unthinkable.

There has already been much written and pondered about as regards Inception in the relatively short running time of its life. One can only imagine what will be written and said about it in ten years time. For although it's arguably a bit too early to be talking about it being held in such high regards as the likes of 2001: A Space Odyssey, it's inescapable that Nolan's movie is this current generation's sci-fi classic. That Nolan has managed to make it accessible to the mainstream, and dazzled the eyes as much as the brain in the process, is close to being a piece of genius craftsmanship.

Inception is a film that it's better to know nothing about before venturing into it, and then it asks, well Nolan asks, for your undivided attention. It's neither as confusing as some have painted it, nor does it have any tricks-peek behind the curtain type-up its sleeve. The truth is is that Inception has something for everyone; thematically speaking, and that's before we pore over the special effects that sees Nolan raising the bar considerably. As is the case with twisty high concept movies, interpretations are many, with the director rightly abstaining from discourse about his movie. What forms the basis is your basic life and death struggles, with the grey areas during and after given a clever cinematic make over. There's also meditations on grief that this reviewer personally found easy to get involved with; that of course wont work for everyone, but that is just one of many strands that Nolan dangles for the discerning viewer.

If that all sounds a bit too serious for the man who has redefined the Super Hero genre, rest assured thrill seekers, Inception is also a loud swirly spectacle. The action is raucous, be it gun fights or zero gravity punch ups, Nolan has not lost the ability to take the viewer on an action fuelled roller-coaster ride, aided superbly by Lee Smith's editing and Pfister's perfectly broad photography While Zimmer's score blends electronic action pulse beats with saddened guitar strains (ex-Smiths guitarist Johnny Marr on 12 string) to craft one of the best scores of 2010. As I said, there's something for everyone here, making it perhaps one of the leading nominees for title of ultimate modern day blockbuster.

Then there's the strong ensemble cast, led by a quite scintillating performance from DiCaprio. Following on from his cards played close to his chest turn in Shutter Island, DiCaprio has given 2010 two of its best lead performances. Here he gives real depth of emotion, the kind that makes it easy for the viewers to hang their hats on. His unfussy acting is easy to buy into, giving the character the air of believability, he is the glue that binds the whole film together. Murphy is wonderfully vulnerable, very much an axis in the narrative, while Levitt almost usurps DiCaprio with a neatly layered portrayal that carries a delightful whiff of duality about it. Special praise, too, for Ellen Page. Still in her early 20s, she exudes an intelligent sexiness that shines bright in a role that could have been boorishly played as a cipher in a lesser actress' hands. While Hardy provides brawny levity and Berenger leaves a favourable mark.

The Matrix meets Heat and Mission Impossible, only it's written by Phillip K. Dick and Richard Matheson; or something like that. A cracking hybrid movie that's fit to grace any summer and sure to improve and enlighten with further viewings.

title: A 9.2/10 dream.
review:
Nolan, Nolan, Nolan. Where do I start?

How can I start?

I have to say that I usually do not refer to other movies while comparing and I'll rate this movie as an experience alone.

Inception by far is the best cinema I have seen to date and I'll tell you why.

The sheer brilliance of it is mind blowing. The idea of corporate espionage via dream sharing is by far the craziest and yet the most spectacular idea of this decade. When I heard about this movie I was like, "Oh cool, another Sci-Fi movie." Then the trailer came out and we saw a whole city bending on its own and I was like, "Gotta watch that movie.".

Inception excels in storyline and visuals better than practically every other movie. The sheer idea of nested dream sharing is beyond the thinkable and the execution of the movie is remarkable. By far Nolan's best work, and even as a Nolan fan from the era of The Dark Knight, I have to say, this movie exceeds even his own The Dark Knight in many ways. First off, this movie explores the mind itself in ways that allows us to visualize what our subconscious thinks. The movie gives us a better understanding of ourselves as humans and truly is a remarkable feat of cinematography. The sheer ambition of the movie itself is enough to get you on the edge of your seat. Leave the visuals, the scoring is daunting. Hans Zimmer at work again uses the tick tock metronome again to perfection and the blaring horns that make us fall off our seats. And who even expected that JACK from the Titanic would end up performing the role of an Corporate Thief perfectly? The acting is beyond sublime and truly the movie Inception is by far my favorite movie till date.

However, Inception does lack minorly. There are a few plotholes in the movie, but in the expanse of less than three hours, their is very little Inception doesn't achieve. If anything the only place where Inception lacks is in character development and storyline. I have so little against this movie and I have to say, this movie is a feat in cinematic history.

Overall, this movie is a must watch for anyone. An incredible thriller and emotional story. Inception truly delivers an awesome cinematic experience.

And so, the inevitable: Paprika vs. Inception. Really? You didn't see that coming? A lot of people seem to think this movie is wonderful. It has star power, I suppose, and a lot of people like stars. To me, it looked like half a dozen Japanese animes slapped together into an incomprehensible mishmash mess, combined with some thinky dialog that supposedly glues it all together. Crap, in other words.

I read the Wikipedia article on this movie, just to make sure I didn't miss some profound thing that would change my mind. Even the article was dull and uninspiring...I read the first and last paragraph, and that was a chore. I'm not picky...if I'm entertained, I'm happy, even if the plot/acting/whatever sucks. I'm sure the acting was great, the special effects were awesome, and the key grip showed others how it's done. I just couldn't get in to this movie. I didn't care if the main characters lived or died, I didn't care if the McGuffin got got, and I didn't care if the stupid top fell over. Despite Hollywood's slobbering over this movie, you might notice nobody bothered to make a sequel or otherwise capitalize on its greatness. Was that because they didn't want to defile its artistic purity? Um, not likely. It's trash, and Tokyo knows it.

title: My Re-Review of Inception: It's Chris Nolan's Best Film; And My All-Time Favourite!
review:
Inception is what cinema wants the audience to feel and more: a dream that ceases to be fake on every conceivable level. It's a meta-film that comes full circle with its implications as to what the audience can take away from a truly impactful movie, whether all the story was a dream or not, whether most of it actually happens until a certain point, or whether the story has no 'right' way to interpret it.

The story is relatively simple for Cobb: he's a man trying his best to clear his name and return to his family in America, and he needs to plant an idea into the mind of a media mogul's son about to inherit his father's empire. The rest is something else entirely; Cobb is a master 'dream-thief' who has inner demons of his own and he keeps these demons at bay even if it means risking the mission at hand.

Inception is a blockbuster that has the makings of an art film populating an action-adventure story, and making the absolute best of the scenes Nolan's given. This film has classic moment after classic moment; the dream-elevator, the rotating hallway scene, the car-chase, the snow fortress and Limbo make for some of the film's many golden moments. The set pieces are amazing, the direction is flawless and the imagery does evoke the sensation of dreaming. Nolan makes his films have a beating heart to them and Inception is full of it through and through.

Inception is the kind of reason that I can say is the reason I love movies. From its ambitious story to intricately done characters and set-pieces add up to one of the most well-made films to ever grace the planet. This is Nolan at his very best; and more!

Inception gets 5/5 gold-stars.

The beauty of the movie is that the audience is left with their own interpretations on the fate of the characters. Because the top continues to spin, one may assume he is still in the dream, which may lead them to find the astonishing ending as sad seeing that he is doomed in the dream space missing out on the lives of his children. One may view Leonardo being stuck in the dream as a happy ending because throughout the rest of the film he avoided his responsibilities to his family and job to find his deceased wife in dark areas of his mind. This perspective of ending would allow Dicaprio to be with not only his children, but his wife. I don't like most of that idea because he finally was able to let go of her and a happier version may be the other option the viewers may experience which is one in which he escaped the dream. The film comes to an end with the top spinning, however it does begin to wobble and may appear to some as beginning to fall. With this view, Leonardo has conquered his darkest fears and the crew accomplished their mission and can live his life free from worry with money and what was left of his family. However, with the knowledge that Christopher Nolan is quite a dark and mysterious man it is apparent that he wanted the audience to interact with the film and for them to decide whether they wanted the ending to be melancholiac or euphoric as a sort of emotional experiment. The audience was meant to be left not with the question of whether the top falls or not but how do their lives and depictions of the film change the fates and storyline of Inception. Inception itself is defined as a starting point, perhaps a starting point in knowing the furthest reaches of the human mind, not that of DiCaprio's character but of the audience members. The film is tragic and breathtaking and one must take it for what it is.

But the top does continue to spin.

title: Awesome Effects, Try and Keep Up!
review:
Cristopher Nolan's Inception is quite grasping in the sense that you can't look away for long or you may lose your grip on the storyline. There are plenty of action packed scenes with out of this world digital effects to keep your attention, but the reason we lock our eyes to this film is truly to keep up with it. Taking us in and out of many of the characters including Dom Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio), Arthur (Joseph Gordon-Levitt), Mal (Marion Cotillard), Mr. Saito (Ken Watanabe), and Robert Fischer's (Cillian Murphy) dream state and subconscious, we are forced to engage the analytical portions of our brain in an effort to stay with the story. 
The overall theme of the movie came in mixed signals, leaving me initially unable to decide whether the film was centered around corporate espionage, a father's willingness to do anything to see his children, or learning to let go of the past. After some more thought, I have to go with a father's willingness to do anything to see his children again. Mostly due to the fact that the majority of the film in which they are trying to plant an idea in Robert Fischer's head was spawned as a result of the decision Dom made to accept the job in an effort to see his children again. Thereafter and even before, there are scenes that cut to projections of his children as he can't seem to shake them or his dead wife's subconscious projection. The dream glow lighting effects used in these projections of his children are enough to make you feel his pain and sadness further emphasizing the reason he has taken an almost impossible job to get back to them. These repetitious projections provide a motif that is evenly spread throughout the film in an effort to remind us why he is there in the first place.
As you are taken either gracefully or forcefully from one scene to the next in the many altered dream state realities, Cristopher Nolan does a fantastic job making sure part of you goes with the character while you also remain thoughtful of the true reality of the dreamer and those along for the ride. The digital effects in most scenes are astounding and the thoughtful use of various speeds of slow motion to produce the effect and understanding of their dream state was masterfully done. This is especially apparent during the crux of the film as they immerse themselves into a three-level deep dream state in which each level's time passes differently in hours, days, months, or years! Overall, this film is a pretty mind-blowing work of art that goes way beyond our imagination to show just how far a father will go for his children.

title: Awesome
review:
Inceptions is one of the biggest hits of 2010 that will leave you questioning your own reality. Directed by Christopher Nolan, the film stars Leonard DiCaprio as Cobb, as a thief (extractor) that specializes in industrial espionage, but in a very unique way... he steals the information from his targets own mind in their dreams. Cobb is hired by Saito, Ken Watanabe, to pull off inception, or planting an idea in someone's mind. In this case Saito wants the son of one his business rivals, Robert Fischer (Cillian Murphy), to break up his father's company upon his death. In order to complete this job, Cobb needs the help of his five member team. The first team member is Author, played by Joseph Gordon-Levitt. He is the researcher of the team, and finds out all the details of the target to make the information extraction easier. The next member of the team is Eames played by Tom Hardy. Eames is the team's forger, which means he can impersonate anyone while in the dream world. The third member of the team is architect Ariadne, who is played by Ellen Page. Her job is to design the mazes in the dream world in order to give them extra time to complete the inception. Dileep Ra, plays Yusuf, the chemist and final member of the team who designs and administers a sedative that helps keep the team and the target asleep, while not diminishing brain functions. 
 The main theme of Inception is that of emotional effect. This is most clearly demonstrated by how Cobb is portrayed in the film. He and his wife Mal, portrayed by Marion Cotillard, had previously been stuck in limbo. In order to get out, Cobb implants the idea in his wife head that she is stuck in the dream world. This works to well, and once they get out she is unable to accept that she is in the real world. She believes it so much that she sets up a scene of her "murder" and waits for Cobb to arrive. Then she tells him that he has to kill himself with her so they can go back. If not, he will be blamed for her murder and spend the rest of his life in jail. Cobb refuses to do it even as she jumps to her death. Cobb is now forced to be on the run and separated from his kids.
 Visually, Inception is very similar to his previous films of the Prestige, and Memento. They all have the dark color pallets, and intense visual images. One of the strongest visuals in this film is the mirror scene in the dream world. This scene hints that there could be infinite levels to the dream world. I believe it reinforces the idea that even the "real world" is also a dream world that Cobb is stuck in. The other effect worthy of note is the use of slow motion. I believe that the use of slow motions adds to the audience experiencing the time change compared to the dream world. 
Overall, I believe that the Inception is a visually stunning film that is definitely worth the 2 hour and 28 minute run time.

title: Christopher Nolan has created a masterpiece
review:
SPOILERS!
The name Christopher Nolan has become synonymous with amazing Hollywood films in recent years. They see him as a man who can simply direct a movie that will entertain the masses. However, few truly understand his genius. On the contrary, Christopher Nolan knows how to portray abstract ideas on the big screen better than anyone. For the truth is that there are plenty of directors who can make an engaging movie that people will like. Christopher Nolan presents abstract ideas about dreams in the the movie "Inception" using beautiful cinematography and clear plot devices such as timing and layering that keep the audience engaged and thinking.
I think Inception is a great film for a few reasons: the cinematography is amazing, the cast is stellar, it is action packed, and it visualized abstract ideas. The cinematography captures the amazing settings such as that of the street of Paris, France and the beautiful arctic mountains of Kananaskis Canada. Christopher Nolan also took the time to shoot scenes using practical effects rather than using CGI. This makes the movie seem more realistic and interesting. He builds set with impossible shapes like the Penrose Steps and a stairwell loop. Using camera tricks and editing he is able to make the impossible look possible. Movie that rely on CGI rather practical effects provide a more realistic feel to a film that CGI, in all its 21st century glory, can't do justice.
The cast of Inception is a recipe for success. The cast consists of only the best actors that have a history for making good movies. Leonardo DiCaprio the main protagonist has been in good films since he was like 15 years old when he was in "What's Eating Gilbert Grape" with Johnny Depp. Other consistently successful actors such as Joseph Gordan-Levvit, Ellen Page, and Tom Hardy play supporting characters throughout the film. The chemistry between them on top of the skillful acting results in a realistic movie that engulfs you into the plot of the movie.
The movie also has a lot of action in it. Inception is essentially a heist movie, but they are planting something in someone's mind instead of trying to steal something. There are guns, goons, car chases, and explosions. A recipe for any good action movie. The action in the plot keeps the story interesting and you never know what will happen next. The realism and griminess of shootouts in the rain and show the character of the film. The scenes are filmed together collectively and not jump cut every second which let the seems flow and become drawn out. This allows it not to feel shaky and stitched together. The action allows more audience members to enjoy the movie even if not in tune with the intellectual concepts of the film.
The last reason I believe Inception is one of the greatest movies of all time is because of the topic. The main plot-line of the movie involves dreams, an abstract idea, that becomes visualized in the film. Dreams are something that everyone can relate to. Dreams have been a controversial topic for many years. The ancient Egyptian Pharaohs believed they could predict the future and was a way to communicate with the Gods. We have learned much about the neural activity that actually control dreams in the twenty-first century, but dreams still have an unpredictable mystery that fascinates many with still more to be discovered about them. It shows the weirdness of dreams and give an explain of the psychology behind sharing dreams and the effects it can have.
Some people argue against the genius of "Inception." A point made against it is: "How come when they went to Limbo, it was in DiCaprio's mind?" First of all, it is explained in the movie that if you create enough dream layers you will fall into "Limbo." They state in the dialogue of the movie when a character gets shot that if he dies, they are so heavily sedated that he won't wake up, he will fall into Limbo. However, when he falls into Limbo he will be exposed to whatever was created in the Limbo state by anyone else who has been there before in their shared dream. This is only DiCaprio's character because he went there with his wife when exploring the power of shared dreaming. This person simply was not paying attention to the film and did not understand what was going on. His incompetence shouldn't be costing this movie a bad rating.

title: My favorite Nolan film to date...
review:
Plot

Inception is a heist film that features Leonardo DiCaprio as a Dominic "Dom" Cobb who has been forced to leave the States due to a murder conviction. This event leaves him desperately trying to find his way back to his kids, while pulling one extraction job after another just to make ends meet. These are no ordinary extraction jobs, however, since Cobb is using a highly experimental military technology that allows him to infiltrate the mind of his target and ultimately manipulate that person into giving him the information that he needs to successfully complete the mission. When Cobb's first job in the film goes wrong and he fails in his assignment, he is ultimately forced to work with a Japanese billionaire businessman, played by Ken Watanabe, who promises Cobb a chance to finally return to America and be with his children. The biggest catch of the deal is that Cobb must pull off a job that is otherwise considered impossible to do. He must plant an idea into the mind of his target, played by Cillian Murphy, that will compel the latter to make a major business decision that would disband his father's energy company, a method known as Inception.

The Casting

The casting for this film is spot on. Leonardo DiCaprio is unforgettable as a broken, yet highly clever and experienced extractor of information who just wants to go home and be reunited with his family.

Cobb's right-hand man, Arthur (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) is very suave and competent in his field as he as constantly attempts to appeal to Cobb's more logical reasoning by offering up a more realistic viewpoint of the latter's situation. Arthur is particularly skeptical of not only Saito's intentions but also of whether Inception is even a possibility. Believing the mission to be a massive failure from the start, Arthur tries to convince Cobb to simply walk away from the job, despite Saito's irresistibly tempting offer.

The rest of the casting in Inception is perfect. Christopher Nolan couldn't have done a better a job of assigning these roles if he'd tried.

Pacing

The movie includes an excellent combination of fast-paced action scenes and a more deeply written story that focuses on the individual development, agendas, and flaws of some of the characters. Nolan's approach to exploring the sub- consciousness of one's mind and how it can be manipulated by an outside force is enough to make me appreciate the unexpected twists and turns in the plot itself as my mind races and my heart continues to pump nonstop throughout the course of the film all the way to the end.

The Story

It's so easy to make an action film all about the action or to make a deep, emotional film all about the story and maybe not include enough action, but that isn't a problem for Inception. Nolan gives us a compelling story that focuses on the visceral depth of the characters and the challenges that they face throughout the course of the film, while simultaneously using the action only to support the continuous flow of the story, instead of overshadowing it with too many pointless explosions, fight, and/or car chase scenes. Yes, the film does include all of this, but it is never overwhelming or entirely pointless. The Story With Inception, we get a fresh, complete original and engaging story that never fails to impress. Personally, I feel that it leaves me with an ending the makes me think about the limitations of my imagination and where I can go with that imagination if I just knock down the barriers that would otherwise keep me from going to distance and beyond with my own vision. From beginning to end, the story keeps the viewers guessing. It keeps them wondering and, therefore, constantly trying to figure out what is real and what is just another part of the dream. It will force you to ask questions, intelligent questions that could alone prove to be a roller-coaster ride of a trip for the mind itself. What is real? What isn't real? Is any of it real, or are all the characters in this film leaving in one big dream world? These are the questions that I find myself asking during and after watching this masterpiece of a film.

Visual Appeal

Visually, the greatest highlights of the film were of course the city scene, which showed us a dreamed-up Paris bending into itself, and the hotel scene, which showed us constantly rotating and shifting environment that basically said, "Reality, what's that?" Watching a film like Inception, I can't help but wonder if maybe I'm living in a dream world half the time. Who knows, maybe somebody else is bending my so-called reality to their will so they can extract valuable information from the sub-conscious reaches of my mind.

Final Verdict

Inception is completely original both in concept and in execution of that concept. There is absolutely no point of failure in either the story, the character development, or the general pacing with this film. So, if you enjoy the kind of science-fiction, psychological thrillers that toy with the mind's understanding of the very definition of reality itself, then, this is an A-grade movie that will not fail to live up to your expectations. I give this film a rating of 10 out of 10 for best performances, best story, and best originally done visuals that I've seen in a long time.

As for an artistic value this film did an exceptional job at connecting the viewers to the plot with well thought out camera shots as well as lighting and sound. Next we will look at Entertainment value, the film has been awarded in several different categories. It is an intricate but fast paced plot that keeps you from getting bored or distracted. The last value we will look at is the Literary value, the success of the theme and the meaning behind just another exciting action movie. There could be several themes combed out of this film but a quite obvious one is that our loved ones are never truly gone. We see this when Cobb's is in the deepest layer of the movie and he explains to Mal he couldn't create her as beautiful as she was with all of her imperfections and flaws. He was hurting himself more by keeping her there and he needed to let her go.

In conclusion Inception does an excellent job at presenting all four values into the film keeping it entertaining, artistic, educational but also full of meaning. It has excellent cinematography and unique shots paired with talented actors to give the audience the puzzled effect the director Nolan desired. I would give this film a 9 out of 10.

title: A masterpiece that made me realize something. Fellow writers, read on. No spoilers.
review:
It's 2017 and I finally managed to watch Inception, twice at that. Seven years after its release, I don't think it's necessary to go over the qualities of this movie again and bore you with expletives and superlatives regarding its excellence. The rating and the rest 2000+ reviews can tell you enough about that. Instead, I decided to present you with a fresh view on Inception's essence - my own one. Stay with me and I promise you that by the end of this review, you'll see yet another layer of Inception you haven't even thought about.

After seeing Inception for the second time, I realized that the primary concept of the movie - ideas, is in fact an elaborate tutorial on writing fictional characters.

Inception explores ideas and the way they affect us. In our everyday lives entering one's dreams and implanting an idea would be an impossible task. However, there is one place in real life (or not so real life) where inception of ideas is inevitable - books.

The author of a book isn't much different from the extractors in Inception. Because the author always works within his character's mind. He must know who his character is better than anyone else, in order to know who they will become by the end of the story.

In the course of the narrative, the author leads the character along a path that foreshadows and shows them hints about the future outcome. Nothing else - just hints. The character must arrive at the designated outcome by themselves. Thus, they go through the specifically constructed challenges and obstacles, which urge them to look at the world from a different angle and maybe realize a thing or two about themselves and the people around them. The author never explicitly says "See what I did here? It's supposed to lead to this and that." because that would break the willing suspension of disbelief of both character and reader - it would draw attention to the writer. However, he covertly (and cleverly) weaves the path before his character and shows them the things that would make them question themselves and eventually lead to a change in their mindset.

Yet, what drives the character forward after all? Their goal. But, let's face it - no character goal is truly that character's personal goal. Literary characters are just that - fiction. In reality, goals belong to the author who masks them so skillfully that the character believes them to be their own. After all, goals are the embodiment of a character's hopes and dreams and although their material form is usually absent at the beginning of the story, the strive to achieve them gives the character strength and perseverance. And what else in the world is intangible, yet strong enough to affect one's life? Ideas.

If you are just reading books for enjoyment and not obsessively inspecting each sentence like I do, at the end of the story you will see a character that has altered their way of thinking, but you won't realize the process through which it had happened. They would have either reached their goal, or realized that it hadn't been what they actually needed. Anyway, they would be a "new person" - they would look at the world with clear eyes. When you trace it back in the story, you might be able to tell how and why (provided that you are skilled enough in literary analysis).

But why is it so hard to determine the trigger of character development WHILE you are reading? Let's make it clear - it's not because you're not paying attention. A badly written story will scream "THIS IS SUPPOSED TO LEAD TO CHARACTER DEVELOPMENT!" ten pages before the actual trigger. Then what is the secret?

The thing is, just major story events strung together can't lead to character development that feels natural and the story will start screaming for attention like I showed above. Moreover, characters will be one-dimensional, will seem to lack firm motivations and goals, and their emotions will feel forced.

The secret lies in the small details skillfully placed at just the right moments in the narrative, which build upon one another to lead to the major events. Thereafter, the major events have greater impact and resonate into character development. Amateur writers won't notice these essential small details unless they have trained themselves to spot them through reading. They will think that the major events are the only triggers of character development. Then they will write their own stories without these key details and wonder why they won't trigger the same emotions like their favorite novels. Why they won't trigger any emotions at all. Well, now you know why.

Anyway, I feel my review turned into a creative writing lecture, but Inception perfectly illustrates the way an author develops their characters. At least that's the conclusion I reached for myself and the way I saw the movie. Because I'm a writer and I filter everything through my own crazy, maniacal, writing prism. My review may not appeal to the people who came for the action sequences or the ones who simply wanted to enjoy a masterfully crafted story. However, I hope my point will reach those of you who are just as literary crazy as I am.

I would prompt you to read this review after you've watched the movie, so you can see the connection between what I said and what happened in the story. Though since I'm placing this paragraph at the end of my review, it would be foolish to ask this of you, won't it? Yet again, I would prompt you to reread it after you've seen the movie. Or at least, to go into Inception with the idea in mind that it is an illustrative example of how to develop characters in fiction. The best of all examples.
