title: A feast for the eyes, mind, and heart
review:
Striking a truly impressive balance between engaging the mind, the heart, and the heart rate, Inception is the first movie since The Dark Knight that I wanted to see again the very next day (no coincidence since they were made by the same person). It has been said that Hollywood relies too much on special effects to cover lazy storytelling; not so with Inception, where truly stunning visuals only supplement what you'll really be talking about: the story, what it means, how it moved you, and how shockingly original it is. I've never seen anything like it, either in concept or in narrative structure. Neither have I attended, in a long time, a film that gave my brain such a workout.

This is a movie that expects you to pay attention and make connections. Leonardo DiCaprio gives a heartbreaking performance, leading a cast of top-notch actors playing interesting characters in a film that appears to be a science-fiction action/heist caper (a rather unique concept in itself), but is actually about guilt, the desire for redemption, and the raw power of simple ideas. Director Christopher Nolan, as he did with Batman Begins and The Dark Knight, takes something fantastic and paints it in realistic tones. This is what unbridled imagination, combined with intelligence, emotion, and talent looks like on film. It is mentally and emotionally challenging. It also has some terrific action (including a physics- bending fight sequence that is jaw-dropping) and is very creative in its use of cinematography, editing, and music. Though comparatively light on language, with no sexual material and action violence where physical harm is not what's at stake (you'll understand when you see it), Inception is nonetheless not recommended for anyone younger than teens due to its complexity and intense subject matter.

title: Review of the Cinematography of Inception
review:
Imagine you are dreaming, and you know it. You are an architect and have the power to do anything you want to your landscape. You can build skyscrapers or farm houses, you can make oceans appear out of nothing, and you can defy the laws of physics. You can go into the deepest spaces of your subconscious and see all of your fears, secrets, and desires. You can dream voluntarily and even bring other people along with you. This is Inception. Leonardo DiCaprio acts as Cobb, a thief who steals much more than everyday material items. He has the capability to steal secrets from the minds of other people through their subconscious, by invading their dreams without them knowing. While this sounds amazing, it is an enormous power to have, and with great power comes great responsibility. Cobb gets involved in a dangerous mission and is asked to plant an idea into another person's mind. He has already lost his family to his career, but if he completes this task, he could get it all back. However, he is not prepared for the emotional baggage he's kept to appear at work. Inception is a complete and total enigma. It is anything and everything that one could ever possibly imagine, but never think of themselves. It is so original in itself that there is nothing remotely close to being like it. It deserves every accolade and testimonial it is given, and while director Christopher Nolan is very responsible for that, he was not alone in creating this masterpiece.

Wally Pfister is a cinematographer and director who is well known for his work with Christopher Nolan. In Inception, he uses cinematography to tell a story. It's not just about getting the perfect shot, it's about connecting the audience to the picture and the actors. With pristine clarity from every angle, viewers are immediately immersed in their surroundings. He draws them in by giving each shot a unique look from the next. Because of Inception's complicated plot line, he uses color, lighting, and shot types to his advantage in differentiating environments from one another. The component of the film that is most obvious to the viewer is lighting. In the first scene, the audience sees waves on the beach crashing into the shore. Pfister uses natural light to portray the outdoors and create a bright environment. In the next, viewers see Leonardo DiCaprio being led inside a dark building. Here, Pfister uses a dim palette with warm colors to show both the change of environment as well as the different emotions of each scene. This pattern continues as the plot unravels throughout the film.

One particularly great shot Pfister uses to engage his audience is an aerial view of the environment. For the majority of the film, when the characters move into a new setting, viewers are graced with a breathtaking overhead shot of their surroundings. These wide pans show a boundless space, but usually always have a focal point. For example, while the audience sees a large, urban city that becomes the next setting of the story, they can't help but to be focused in on a small, bright helicopter flying over top of it. After seeing these wide shots viewers are drawn in once again through medium shots and close ups. Pfister also knows the importance of camera movement in the story. He constantly uses shaky camera movement when characters are walking, running, or fighting. He also uses it to make experience more real for viewers. For example, when Leonardo Dicaprio and his supporting cast are in a helicopter, the camera is gently moving, not so much to distract people from what is happening in the scene, but to enhance what is happening in the film. This strategy makes it easy for the audience to get lost in the story and connect to feel like they are in the film themselves.

Another important component of the cinematography that directly relates to the story is the use of cuts. In the story, one of the ways characters realize that they are dreaming is if they cannot figure out how they have gotten to where they are. It seems as if they appear there out of thin air. Each cut pertains to this aspect of the film because they rarely offer information on how characters end up in certain places. This leads the audience to wonder if the characters are really dreaming, or if that is just the way the story is laid out. Overall, Pfister does an amazing job of joining the viewers to the visuals of Inception. He uses cinematography to portray emotion and allow his audience to feel everything going on in the film. He has the power to make people feel something, and without his amazing camera work this never would have happened. Without Pfister, Inception would not be the masterpiece that it is today.

title: Intelligent and Brilliant in Every Moment
review:
Christopher Nolan is one of the best directors of the early 21st century. I don't think there would be many to dispute that fact. Inception is one of the best movies of the early 21st century. I doubt that causes much of a stir either. However when I say that Inception is probably Nolan's best movie to date I'm sure I would get a lot of complaints.

So why is Inception such a masterpiece to even surpass the other works of the 2000's is the skill seen in every aspect of the films creation. From the sound design and musical score that is provided by the master composer Hans Zimmer to the more than praiseworthy cinematography of Wally Pfister who is at his best here in providing some of the most gorgeous shots I have ever seen in a blockbuster film like this one.

I haven't even had time to mention the visuals. There are times in modern day cinema where I feel fatigued of the constant barrage of bad CGI implementation in the movies that are touted as the 'best action movie of the year' that I forget just how much of a beneficial tool it can be when used correctly. This is truly Inception's greatest asset. The many great moments of this film are a mix between the real and practical effects and the computer generated special effects that blur together in such a way that you can barely make the two apart and scenes you'll swear must have been made on a PC are made the way that film makers have been doing for nearly a century. This great uncertainty in what is real and what is not adds magic to this film that has long been becoming a rarity in this age where we truly must marvel in how a scene was done.

The acting is of course as good as one can expect from a cast of this caliber and hold their own among the other heavy hitters.

I beg you to watch this movie if you have not yet. It will remembered in the same class of those that came before from the hands and minds of those like Spielberg, Lucas, and Scorsese.

title: Cob, the protagonist, invades people's dreams and must implant an idea.
review: While some people don't agree that Nolan's Inception deserves to be number 14 pm IMDb's top 250 movies of allÂ time, I think it has many features that make it worthy of such a position. First, however, I must address the one drawback I found with the film. I think there is an objective lack of character development in the movie. Cobb, the main character, is the only character who is not a one dimensional character. The sheer number of secondary characters forces them to compete for screen time and thus hinders their own development. However, this shortcoming is, in my opinion, well outweighed by the other aspects of the film. For example, the complexity of the movie is unparalleled by most blockbuster films. While the exposition may feel contrived at points, I think Nolan challenges the audience's intellect. Many viewers need to watch the movie more than once just to fully grasp the plot. Secondly, the ambiguity of the movie opens it up to multiple interpretations, and gives film with a lasting impact on the viewer. Personally, I think a movie that has you thinking about its meaning far beyond your first viewing experience is a great movie. For example, to some viewers the movie seems to suggest that the movie itself was all a dream, but to others it may not seem so. But there is evidence for both sides. An example for the former theory is when Cobb returns to his children, and they tell him that they've been building a "house on a cliff", which is strongly associated with Saito's dreams (another secondary character), hinting at the possibility of the movie ending in a dream. However, evidence also points to the contrary, such as Cobb's wedding ring only appearing in scenes that are dreams. It's the ambiguity that allows the movie to resonate with its viewers, and it's why the film is so widely praised. Furthermore, the soundtrack deserves its share in credit. Not only does it take risks by being a pronounced part of many emotional scenes, but it was actually crafted from a single piece of music: the "French song" that signifies the end of a dream. Overall, despite its shortcomings in character development, I think this film deserves much of its critical praise, because it is complex enough to to satisfy a viewer many times over.

title: INCEPTION Review - Buildings tilt. Streets coil. Characters float.
review:
Christopher Nolan's "Inception" is one of the most best directed and looking movie you will ever watch. Are you awake? Or are you asleep? That is the question you will be asking yourself throughout the movie, and we will never truly know. Inception is a movie where buildings tilt. Streets coil. Characters float.

Leonardo DiCaprio conducts a team of high risk takers (or criminals depending on which way you look at it) who delve deep into a target's dreams, having numerous detours, good and bad. To get it out there straight away, the film itself is not for everyone, due to the high-complex storytelling that Nolan is presenting. Yes, this is one of those movies that will confuse you if you don't pay attention from start to finish.

The basic pot of"Inception" revolves around Dom Cobb (DiCaprio!) who is an expert at entering victims' dreams and "extracting" secrets through heir subconscious. Cobb cannot return home for certain reasons (Spoiler free review). He is approached by a powerful and wealthy businessman (Watanabe) who wants Cobb to "flip" his common pursuit and instead embed an idea in someone's mind.

Dom is required to enter the dreams of Fischer (Murphy) and persuade him to disassemble it to Watanabe's desire, with ultimately a return home. Cobb is joined by Arthur (Gordon-Levitt), Ariadne, an architect (Page) who constructs the dream worlds; Eames, a forger (Hardy) who can portray anyone at will; and a pharmacist (Rao) who enables very deep sleep.

The idea of Inception isn't as putting the victim to sleep for 10 hours. The team and their client not only enter the same dreams, but "enter dreams within his dreams and dreams, within those dreams". In other words, 10 hours turn into 10 years at the bottom level of the dream (limbo).

Christopher Nolan's "Inception"is a movie that won't disappoint any viewer, as long as they are prepared to sit down and watch this movie without any breaks or stops, as you will be immediately lost and / or confused about what is going on. My personal rating for this movie is a 9.9 / 10 and after watching this masterpiece, the high rating can easily be agreed with.

title: A dream within a dream within a log upon a stream
review:
I had seen this film three times in the theater, and countless other times on the small screen, and I still notice little things that are new to me. Unlike in The Matrix where the plot goes nowhere, Inception has layers in its storytelling that forces the viewer to question everything that is happening on screen. I have come to the conclusion that the entire movie is a single dream narrative, and many red herring's are used to mislead the viewer into separating the film's "reality" and "dream" narratives. There is no reality in this movie; all of what the viewer is seeing is a constant dream state that either Cobb himself is experiencing, or perhaps another party is experiencing. Perhaps someone has infiltrated Cobb's mind and planted the idea that inception was possible -therefore Incepting the idea of Inception in Cobb's mind. Perhaps Mal is the culprit, but I cannot know for sure.

Many people see Inception as a metaphor for filmmaking, as many great films provoke thought and "plant" ideas in the minds of its viewers. Inception is fantastic at planting ideas in the viewers mind in an attempt to redirect the truth. But, the viewer can never know what the truth is. Is the spinning top Cobb's or Mal's totem? What is Cobb's totem if the spinning top was used as a red herring. Man, Inception is even planting ideas in my head now. A truly thought provoking film.

The only gripe I have with this movie is that the characters spout constant exposition, but perhaps that was the point. The exposition in this film is used as a red herring to plant ideas in the viewers mind about how the dream states work- even if they are completely untrue. Don't take anything at face value in this movie. They are trying to pull an Inception on you!

title: Inception
review:
Christopher Nolan specializes in making smart films for mass audiences, and he succeeds completely once again. Not only does Nolan take a complex concept and make it easily digestible and also consistently entertaining, but he squeezes in a bit of a character study as well.

OK, yes, the rest of the characters besides Cobb are all pretty much just plot devices, but they are all completely necessary for the film to work as well as it does. That doesn't mean the characters are just cardboard walls that spout information of course. They are still infused with some character, but they are all pretty much one shade besides Cobb. Cobb originally takes the job of Inception, which he said was impossible, and secretly doesn't want to do because he believes it is how he killed his wife, because he wants to get back to his children rather than be "an old man waiting to die alone". He has been exiled because his family believes he killed his wife, but deep down, Cobb does too. He still wants to be able to go back and change things, which is why he keeps his subconscious version of his wife, Mal, locked within cages of his memories. He uses his free time to explore his past memories and pretend she is still alive, but Mal is just a representation of his guilt over killing her, rather than actually her. This guilt is so powerful that his memories of her (and his children) burst through into other's dreams, notifying their subconscious that he is being controlled. This adds an extra layer of tension to every moment. But eventually, Cobb is forced to confront his subconscious version of her, and accepted that she is dead, and move on to live with his children. That is what the famous ambiguous ending is actually saying. The point isn't whether he is awake or asleep. It's that he no longer cares about that. He simply wants to move on and finally be able to love his children again, without ever looking back or feeling guilty about his past sins.

Film was also the perfect medium for this idea. Think about how every time it cuts and a character is in a completely new place, we simply assume they just got there somehow. This film plays on that by telling us that if you can't remember where you came from, you could be dreaming. That is what makes that moment with Cobb and Ariadne at the market so mind blowing. Also, towards the end, when the film is frequently cutting between the 3 or 4 dream locations that they are in it often uses color to identify immediately which one we are in, so it never gets confusing or muddled. The first dream is blue from rain, the hotel dream is lit yellow, and the third layer is white with snow. Much of the fourth layer is done without cutting back to the others, but we immediately realize that Cobb is in the fourth layer, so once we see Cobb we know. It's simple things like this that makes this complex concept easy. There are also many hints that they are in a dream in the opening scene, such as the beach, the time slowing, and Mal, long before we find out how it all works. Then of course there are the fantastic action set pieces, such as the mind blowing and original spinning hallway scene, and the tense chase scene that leads to a tight squeeze through two buildings. The film works on every level. I just can't imagine a person who wouldn't like this film.

title: a powerful film with a powerful concept.
review: Every once in a while a film finds its way across our screens that challenges us on several levels. Such films challenge us to think critically and pay attention. Others address issues that shake the core of human emotion. Additional films attack our senses with amazing visuals, a powerful score, or both. Christopher Nolan's Inception is a film that takes all of these elements in and turns them into a powerhouse of human emotion. The film explores the theme of the power of guilt and its subsequent ability to overtake everything that makes you yourself, while also making you question what the word reality truly means. The film stars the always powerful Leonardo DiCaprio as the films main protagonist Dom Cobb. Cobb is a man on the run from his past as well as from the country he calls home, struggling to cope with the loss of his wife and separation from his children. Cobb, along with Joseph Gordon-Levitt's character, Arthur, specialize in the extraction of memories from their victims' subconscious minds. Cobb and Arthur are so skilled at this job that they are invited by their most recent mark. The twist, it is revealed, is that he does not want a memory removed, rather he wants an idea inserted into another's mind; A job that is rewarded with nothing short of Cobb's return to his children. What ensues is Cobb's personal mission to accomplish the seemingly impossible and create perform inception on his intended mark. Inception is a film that utilizes both stunning visuals as well as Hans Zimmer's ever powerful score to navigate not only the gravity of the situations Cobb and company find themselves in, but also to explore the depth of emotion that the film resides in. Similar another seminal piece of Nolan film, Interstellar, Inception is a visual and musical delight that attacks the senses and connects the viewer(s) to the experience of the film. These films are also similar in the way that Nolan utilizes cinematography to address the theme of the film. Camera angles are a central focus in Inception, and Nolan uses them masterfully to shift focus from characters to more abstract items that help gain an attachment from his viewers on the concept of totems and their appearance. Inception is viewed by many as a masterpiece from Christopher Nolan. If begs the question of when reality stops being reality and when a dream stops being a dream. Inception also addresses the subconscious need for closure and acceptance of reality. This film stands to me as an excellent example of the power of film to excavate the deepest core feelings of the human mind and its ability to cope with its problems.

title: Nolan's Masterpiece
review:
Inception is one of those rare films in the past decade or two that isn't a comic book movie, that has been this re-watchable. And it's not the action or the jokes or even the beautiful sets and locations. It's the story and how much thought Christopher Nolan put into it. From small things like he only wears his wedding ring in a dream to large story points like weather or not the end is truly ambiguous, this film is incredibly detailed to the point where every single time I watch this, I find something new no matter how big it is.

The acting isn't anything phenomenal but it is subtle which isn't always easy. And I'm not saying it's bad, just no Oscar worthy performances here. But I suppose having Leonardo DiCaprio doesn't hurt. I believe this is where Ellen Paige truly got her rise to fame rather than Juno or X-Men. And of course, we need to give proper recognition to Tom Hardy, Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Cillian Murphy for delivering great performances.

Now I don't need to say much about the score because I'm pretty confident that there isn't a single soul on this planet that doesn't like that score. If someone out there does not, note that I said soul so take that as you will. Hans Zimmer elevates every scene with the soft intimate music when it needs to get emotional and the loud music when the scene is action heavy. And also, Time so there's that.

The writing and directing from Christopher Nolan is so superb that we need to put this film on every list of 'Films You Must Study to Become A Filmmaker'. As mentioned, the small sub-plots are done so well, which is rare, and the main plot is explained and executed with both precision and flair simultaneously. It really goes to show the skill that Chris Nolan has with a pen or a keyboard or whatever he uses. The ending is literally shown at the beginning but it doesn't make sense until you get that last scene after Ken Watanabe's character dies. And of course there is the "twist", i'll be it, not a very mind blowing one but it's very sweet and simple. The fact that we learn they were in the dream world for nearly 50 years together and Cobb actually planted the idea that she was in a dream in real life is pretty cool and just makes sense why she killed herself and why Cobb feels so bad. There isn't a single wasted line or scene in this film and I love it.

Of course, film is subjective but to me, this is as close to objectively good as we're going to get in regards to film. I would highly recommend this to anyone interested in the film. It's beautiful, intense, mysterious and fun. Enjoy the film and bring on Dunkirk!

title: One of the Great Modern Spectacles
review:
Leonardo DiCaprio is the last big movie star left in the world. There may be one or two others who can still bring in big crowds, but so what. Being a movie star is about projecting an image. Bogart did that. Dean did that. Brando did that. And so does DiCaprio.

Christopher Nolan is the last big auteur left in the world. No one else can get $150 million original projects off the ground, and no one else can make $150 million projects that are creative and deep and dynamic and appealing to the modern audience. He is our heir to Kubrick and Hitchcock.

So it makes sense that these two team up and make a movie together. And it makes sense that said movie would be one of the greatest pieces of art of the new millennium.

Inception is a movie, but it is far more than that. It is an experience that involves all parts of your mind. There isn't another film that is both this exciting, this interesting, and this intellectually pleasing. It reminds me of the first time I ever heard Beethoven's Ninth or Vivaldi's The Four Seasons.

DiCaprio plays a dream thief. He and his team go into people's heads while they're asleep and steal their memories, such as codes to safes. But a powerful businessman, Saito, offers him a new challenge: inception. He must plant a thought inside the heir to a business fortune and make him believe that he came up with it naturally.

As the film puts it: Arthur: "I say to you, 'Don't think about elephants.' What are you thinking about?" Saito: "Elephants." Arthur: "Right, but it's not your idea. The dreamer can always remember the genesis of the idea. True inspiration is impossible to fake." Despite what Arthur believes at first, inception is not impossible. But it is difficult. Only one man has ever done it before: DiCaprio's character, Cobb. But he never wants to do it again. At first, Saito is put back, but then he makes Cobb an offer he can't refuse. What is this offer? A chance to see his kids again and live in peace. He has been on the run ever since he was accused of killing his wife Mal.

The genius of this film lies in how it dives into Cobb's psyche as he and his team dives into the heir's mind. This pays off time after time, none more so than when the atmosphere gets claustrophobic. It's like eating two decadent cakes stacked on top of each other. If this was done for its own sake, it would be effective but superfluous. But it's not; all the threads come together perfectly.

The cast is incredible. Other than DiCaprio, we have Michael Caine, Tom Hardy, and two of my favorite young stars, Ellen Page and Joseph Gordon-Levitt. I wouldn't say any of them turn in the best performance of their careers, but they are all very good, especially Page, whom I actually connect with more here than I did in Juno.

In any case, this is the best movie most of them will ever be in. And it just gives me a certain fanboyish sort of glee to see some of the best actors alive in one of the best movies of the decade made by one of the greatest living directors.

For most people who haven't seen the movie, the first thing that comes to mind when they think of it is that blaring noise they used in every trailer from 2010-2012. It originated in the trailer for this film and spread like wildfire. That got annoying quickly. But it works in this film. It is shrill and unsettling, which fits the tone of that section of the trailer perfectly. It's no 'Time', a wonderful piece you should check out if you have even a feigning interest in orchestral music. But it is good enough.

That's about how I feel about Zimmer scores in general: even at their worst, they are good enough. The closest I've ever coming to hating a Zimmer score was in Interstellar. That organ grated on me. Yes, it was narratively potent, but poor sound mixing ruined it for me. But most times, I love Zimmer scores. He's the best of the 'new', electronica-influenced composers. His scores in the Batman movies were fantastic. But he is at his best here.

Many people who went to see this movie ended up seeing it two or three times. This is partially because the summer blockbuster season was notoriously vacant, and no other good movies were out. But it is also because this movie confused a lot of people, not in the 'What did I just see?' way, but in the 'That was awesome, but I didn't completely get it, so I'm going to watch it again' kind of way.

This is not Nolan's most confusing and mindbending film- that would be Memento, which I actually and truly did not completely get until I played through it a few times- but it is the most confusing popular Nolan movie. Interstellar comes close, but that movie was more headscratchingly confusing than 'put the pieces of the story together' confusing.

For all the rampant talk about how Nolan's movies lack a heart, this movie works because of its emotional dive into Cobb's heart. Without it, this film is simply a high-concept, amazingly inventive heist film. With it, the film is one of my favorite of all time, a movie I want to break out at every occasion possible.

title: my favourite movie ever
review:
The story can either be told in a few sentences, or not told at all. Here is a movie immune to spoilers: If you knew how it ended, that would tell you nothing unless you knew how it got there. And telling you how it got there would produce bafflement. The movie is all about process, about fighting our way through enveloping sheets of reality and dream, reality within dreams, dreams without reality. It's a breathtaking juggling act, and Nolan may have considered his "Memento" (2000) a warm-up; he apparently started this screenplay while filming that one. It was the story of a man with short-term memory loss, and the story was told backwards.

Like the hero of that film, the viewer of "Inception" is adrift in time and experience. We can never even be quite sure what the relationship between dream time and real time is. The hero explains that you can never remember the beginning of a dream, and that dreams that seem to cover hours may only last a short time. Yes, but you don't know that when you're dreaming. And what if you're inside another man's dream? How does your dream time synch with his? What do you really know?

Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio) is a corporate raider of the highest order. He infiltrates the minds of other men to steal their ideas. Now he is hired by a powerful billionaire to do the opposite: To introduce an idea into a rival's mind, and do it so well he believes it is his own. This has never been done before; our minds are as alert to foreign ideas as our immune system is to pathogens. The rich man, named Saito (Ken Watanabe), makes him an offer he can't refuse, an offer that would end Cobb's forced exile from home and family.

Cobb assembles a team, and here the movie relies on the well- established procedures of all heist movies. We meet the people he will need to work with: Arthur (Joseph Gordon-Levitt), his longtime associate; Eames (Tom Hardy), a master at deception; Yusuf (Dileep Rao), a master chemist. And there is a new recruit, Ariadne (Ellen Page), a brilliant young architect who is a prodigy at creating spaces. Cobb also goes to touch base with his father-in-law Miles (Michael Caine), who knows what he does and how he does it. These days Michael Caine need only appear on a screen and we assume he's wiser than any of the other characters. It's a gift.

Something I've always loved about Donnie Darko is how much it doesn't care if people "get it" or not and it's just as enjoyable no matter how much you understand the film. But, people just say they loved Inception because they didn't get it and don't want to feel stupid. Second, did anybody actually give a s**t about the characters? It makes me sad because if Inception wasn't so obsessed with trying to appeal to everyone; Cobb's amazing backstory could've been handled a lot better. Which leads to my other problem, Christopher really shouldn't have worried about trying to makes this move as accessible as possible. A film like this would work better as a cult film that attracts a certain demographic.

7.5/10 -- Good. Despite all I said, this IS a good movie. It just doesn't deserve #14 (will probably change) on the IMDb Top 250. If you are interested definitely give it a shot but don't let others overhype it for you and if you like movies that make you think, there are plenty of other intelligent films that are as smart as they advertise themselves to be. This is honestly just an action movie in disguise.

title: One of the most ambitious movies ever made.
review:
It's a well-blended mix of big-budget action movie and mind-bender. Like The Matrix, but the story is more tangible than abstract. Cobb (DiCaprio) is tasked with raiding a corporate heir's dreams and organically implanting ideas in them. How he arrives at the premise of helping the host conceive is a mystery the viewer will have to figure out. Telling a story about interconnected layers of dreaming at once was a difficult task, but Nolan pulls it off near flawlessly.

Some action scenes were great, though others should've been pruned to tighten up the pace. I also feel like there could've been less spoonfeeding dialogue. But at the end of the day, you won't find a movie this ambitious that overall comes together so well.

title: Mind Blown!
review:
I remember when I first watched this movie in the theaters and I was just really confused. Some people even left the theater because they were confused! All I knew was that a bunch of characters go into a dream into another dream into another dream in order to accomplish their mission. So I had to watch this movie multiple times in order to understand the ending.

As usual, Christopher Nolan can sometimes mesmerize the audience with mind- blowing, extravagant ideas such as The Prestige and The Dark Knight series. Likewise, Inception has done the same thing once again! Nolan's exciting sci-fi movie starring Leonardo Dicaprio combines the best of modern filmmaking.

Just the thought that other people can "invade" your dreams is actually pretty terrifying and disturbing. The deeper you go into another dream, the harder it is to wake up into the real world. Christopher Nolan came out with this idea when he was 16 years old! Maybe that is why the film is so detail-oriented and mind-boggling! Inception was extremely exhilarating.

One thing that made me and probably many other people confused was its mysterious ending. Will the spinning top keep spinning or was it about to fall over just before the end of the movie? It's up for the audience to decide, but I believe that the spinning top was about to fall. This is because I have watched the movie multiple times and when Leonardo Dicaprio was with his ex-wife, he had a ring on but when he actually saw his kids, there was no ring in his finger. It's just a guess, but I think that is the reason why I believe that Leonardo Dicaprio came back to the real world. What do you think?

97/100

title: THE sci-fi movie of the decade
review:
Last decade we had The Matrix. That was the sci-fi gem of last decade, and it is still pretty awesome. But in the past five years it has had competition because of Inception.

Inception is kind of similar to The Matrix in the way of saying that the world around isn't real. The difference is that the real world IS the real world as we know it, but there is special enhanced "dreaming technology" that is commonly used, originally by soldiers, training in the army, and more recently by architects, of which the main character is one.

Dom Cobb is a single parent, who hasn't seen his two children since shortly after his wife Mal died. She committed suicide, because she had been using the dream technology so much, that she could no longer tell if she was using the dream technology or not.

The plot of Inception is quite complex, and that's what I loved about it. It wasn't just a sit back and relax type of movie. You had to b thinking along with the characters, in order to work out what exactly is going on.

The centre plot piece is that in order to get home Cobb needs to plant an 'idea' into the mind of a business company CEO. To do this, he and his team need to go deep into his (the CEO) subconscious, and discover what's hidden there. However Cobb's wife Mal proves to be a problem as Cobb can't stop thinking about her.

The ending is very ambiguous, but I liked it. It cut out at the last minute, before showing the audience whether Cobb is still dreaming or not. I however guessed he wasn't, due to the evidence supplied throughout the film.

This movie is a complicated sci-fi movie, that is extremely well made, with a complex, but intriguing plot. It is basically, as I said before, this decades Matrix, and for that reason I give it a 9/10

Christopher Nolan does a beautiful job creating and editing this movie to perfection. title: Intelligent and gripping entertainment that remains with you
review:
What many have written as criticism for Nolan's latest cinematic endeavors, I applaud: Christopher Nolan takes himself seriously.

For me, personally, films that attempt to draw me into a story without requiring me to think or even to draw upon more profound emotions and/or intelligence don't remain with me for very long. I want to enjoy a movie in the theater or at home and then keep enjoying it because it's content or portrayal is so compelling that I find mind migrating back to scenes or experiences in the film.

I do enjoy sitting down to a fun, exciting movie solely for the purpose of entertainment. Inception, however, is not one of those movies.

Everyone has dreams. After watching Inception, I found myself musing on the impossibilities and possibilities of dreams. I found myself wanting write down my dreams more often. That's the kind of movie Inception is: the kind that becomes a part, even if it's a small part, of my life. It becomes a place my mind can roam to for engaging thought and feeling. If Christopher Nolan did not take himself or his films so seriously, I'm not sure this level of personal influence could be achievable.

title: Great Movie
review: Inception has a multi-layered plot, quite literally in fact. It focuses on the emotional journey of its lead character, Cobb, but at the same time thrusts the audience into multiple levels of action packed story- telling, very distinct from one another, but all finely connected. It has been described by critics as "a film that rewards intellect", and I can assure you that it is exactly that. Director Christopher Nolan challenges the audience to keep up, and rewards those who can with a breathtaking spectacle, one that has the capability to leave you awestruck. The best part about it is that while you may feel you need to watch it again to be able to fully absorb the experience, chances are, you will probably want to.

title: Inception : Dream or Reality?
review:
Watching Inception was quite a random thing, which turned out to be a very good idea indeed. The viewer is caught by the story from the first scene and does not want to stop watching because of the fear that he might lose some important links between scenes (and worlds, obviously). These are ingeniously linked together, but as the scenes change quickly, it is quite difficult to follow all the story lines in all the different worlds at the same time. That is the most effective skill used by the director - the storyline is explained at the beginning very briefly (and implicitly, as everything else), while the viewer has to put all the pieces of puzzle together by himself. As the story changes suddenly from reality to one world, then back, then another world and so on, it keeps very catchy, because one never knows what is dream and what is real. This is what makes Inception a real masterpiece : it makes people think.

As for the actors, Leonardo DiCaprio was Christopher Nolan's best idea - the truth is that the viewer believes everything to him, even the idea of mastering people's subconscious mind. Despite its unrealistic base, Inception makes a very realistic story which gives you goose bumps. After all, planting an idea in your mind, couldn't it happen to anyone in our modern world?

We could write a whole essay on the actors and say something about every role, how great they were etc. However, the final impression (there is no doubt about that) is made by the music. After Pirates of the Caribbean, Lion King and a wide range of other films, Hans Zimmer shows once again that he is a real expert in emphasizing accurately the atmosphere with minimal music, especially at the end. Quiet, but successful. With his final few notes, we are let to our own minds - does the small top stop turning or not? Is that dream or reality?

title: An individual experience , not comparable to anything else you've ever seen on screen
review:
The events in Inception can be interpreted as a dream generated by Cobbs subconscious to give his traumatic life a meaningful purpose with a comforting ending.

In the real world Cobb gets Mal into drugs. Mal loses her sanity, stops caring about their children and eventually kills herself. Cobb is ridden by guilt (symbolized by the occurring train) for being responsible for his children not having a mother anymore (for having ruined their lives).

From the beginning, the atmosphere breathes with "something just doesn't seem right here" moments throughout the film, without the viewer being able to tell the actual cause. Everything that happens on screen is a dream, with exception of the last scene: Cobb wakes up in a plane, the people around him are all strangers to him. It was his subconscious that made them the protagonists of his dream during his flight home.

The film is Cobb's subconscious trip facing his (symbolic) death. His personal purgatory. As old Saito tells him in the beginning, Cobb is "obsessed with the idea (to come home)": to find peace with Mal, and ultimately forgive himself and find peace in a life reunited with his children. Throughout the film, Cobb can't see (doesn't want to face) the faces of his children, because he isn't ready (yet) to take responsibility for what he had done.

Inception begins with Cobb being given the chance to find peace: Don't you want to take a leap of faith? Or become an old man, filled with regret, waiting to die alone?  Facing old Saito, his personified destiny if he resigns, Cobb accepts the challenge and the trip begins. The solution to Cobb's inner peace lies in himself. In one scene Ariadne (Greek mythology, rather obvious symbol) draws a circular maze, guiding him to the solution: to revisit his innermost traumas and find closure for them.

Ariadne, Arthur and Eames (all the characters with a totem) are Cobb's younger projections of himself. With their help he revisits his own past. The totems are the connection, they represent the different aspects that determine the human life: plain fun, chance (luck), strategy and risk. Life is a game and you are the player.

Cobb relives the key scenes of his life. The actual events remain the same, but Cobb manages to give them a different, comforting context (achieving closure) and a purpose. This corresponds to Charles Eames' "banana leaf parable" and there's your next Name symbolism.

The scene where Robert Fisher forgives his father and recognizes his deep love for him (cries over the paper toy windmill) is the turning point and highlight of the film. At this point, after a tremendous struggle, Cobb forgives himself for letting his children down.

Cillian Murphy's physical resemblance to the young Robert "Bobby" Fischer, the chess player, is so remarkable, Nolan probably could have chosen a less obvious name for his character, to make a point with this symbolic figure. Bobby Fisher was the inventor of a randomized version of chess, that rewards the player for his creativity by giving him many opening possibilities. To win more time to achieve victory, it is necessary for the player to keep making active decisions and keep moving.

Cobb achieves closure with Mal by convincing her (and himself) that they did "grow old together", and he fulfilled his marital promise. It all happened in "Limbo", a metaphorical concept of a different reality.

At the end of the film, it isn't important if the top falls or not, it's important that Cobb left it behind. He overcame his traumas and made peace with himself (forgave himself). He is ready to face his children, meaning that he found absolution.

Many criticized Inception for its complex, hard to follow rules for traveling through the different dream levels. In my opinion, the technical rules of Inception are not important to understand, because Cobb made them up himself (and thus don't need to be consistent or even true). If you had a semester of mathematics, you probably know that on a false premise it's possible to conclude anything.

Emotionally, Inception doesn't strike all of your senses, it's mainly a challenge of and for the mind in proportions and a complexity no one before dared to put in a single film. The extraordinary craftsmanship, the technical skill and the immense care for details, necessary to put a monstrous concept like Inception into a watchable and interesting film are truly amazing.

The most fascinating thing is, that Inception is a brain puzzle that offers several degrees of freedom in trying to fill in the missing parts thus offers you a very individual experience. It remains to be a challenging brain teaser after 5 years. The more you think about it, the more it shows its vast complexity and how much different things there are to discover. The more you think about it, the more you want to watch it one more time. Its greatness and its significance get more and more obvious, the more often you watch the film.

There are tons of symbols to discover during this trip: water, obscured windows, specific colors, watches, names are loaded with symbolism, clothing details, the number 12, Francis Bacon's artwork, usage of many of Carl Jung's concepts, physical resemblances etc, etc. I'm sure I missed a few. Just open your mind and it will come to you.

The key message of Inception is that everyone is the architect (how many times did you hear this word during the film? :-)) of his own fortune. Inception is a very comforting parable of life.

Chapeau, Mr. Nolan. In terms of content, depth and complexity, Inception extends the boundaries of the medium film by a large amount. This is the new benchmark for all future directors to come.

10/10 (Masterpiece)

title: Forrest Gump lives an adventure-packed life.
review: I love this movie! I've watched it at least 10 times. Tom Hanks is an amazing actor and every time I go to Bubba Gump, I get the Forrest Gump vibes. title: Extremely Interesting and Still Entertaining
review:
I'd been told this movie was very forgettable and not really anything special, but I owned it so I thought I should probably watch it. I was and wasn't surprised to find that it was very close to perfection.

Inception is not a movie where you can afford to zone out. You need to pay attention to get the full enjoyment out of this film. I found that I still zoned out at times, but nevertheless understood most of it and was able to enjoy it immensely. It's epic, with interesting characters and a very unique concept.

However, it takes more then a good idea to make a good story. Inception, however, had both. It set itself up to be an epic, yet complicated, movie, and thus it succeeded. It showed the audience that it would be part action right away, which allowed it to make more sense for the plot to involve a good amount of action, and largely revolved around that. Christopher Nolan knew what he was doing with his idea, and that's something that can be hard to find these days.

Overall, Inception is great. I've heard too many people I know say its dumb or nothing special, but I feel like they say that simply because it got high ratings that they may not entirely agree with (or to be the devil's advocate). But when you get down to it, Inception is fantastic. The visuals are great, the concept it great, and overall it's just really well done. Sure, the characters could use work, but that's about the only place where the movie lacked. If your looking to sit down for over 2 hours to think and enjoy something epic, then look no further then Inception.

title: Highly Original Story
review:
Movies like this don't come along that often. Hollywood has come to realize that it is too risky to try and make money off an original idea. In their eyes, it is worth it to make a franchise reboot, or sequel, that is guaranteed to make money.

Director Christopher Nolan provides a breath of fresh air in today's movie scene, including an original story, quality performances, and a breathtaking score.

Inception is the story of Dom Cobb, a very skilled thief, who specializes in using a device to break into people's dreams and extract information. He is infamous for his type of crime and is on the run as the film begins. As the film progresses, the audience finds out that Cobb has been separated from his children for quite some time now, and will do anything to see them again. So, when someone offers him a job which could let him see his children again, he cannot decline. Brace yourself for a total mind trip as Cobb assembles a team to prepare for 'Inception.'

Initially, for a film that is about going into someone's dream and stealing information, it is entirely believable. The philosophy behind the film made me wonder, "Is this actually possible?" Nolan intentionally uses practical effects, something that is very rare to find in modern film. Most filmmakers rely heavily on CGI when they want an impossible shot, Nolan finds ways to do the impossible and excels at it. For example, there is a certain hallway scene in this movie that is 100% practical effects and is shocking how believable it is.

Inception is, quite literally, Nolan's dream. He originally wrote the screenplay while he was writing his first feature film, "Memento." The story isn't based off of a book, or any true events, it is imaginative fiction. It is one that has never been told before and that is what made this movie stand out to me. But no matter how good your effects, direction, or story may be, these don't make a movie, right?

Along with a stellar performance from Leonardo DiCaprio, other such as, Joseph Gordon Levitt, Ellen Page, and Tom Hardy all excel as their established characters. Needless to say, the acting in this movie is very convincing. The movie takes place in multiple different countries; so many of the characters have different dialects. Even with this language barrier, all of the characters still seemed to be coming from the same place and had great chemistry with one-another.

What you hear during a movie is said to be fifty percent of the experience, and Inception's score stands out from the crowd. Composer Han Zimmer and Christopher Nolan seem to always pair up and work together. Han provided the score for all of Nolan's "Dark Knight Trilogy," and 2014's "Interstellar." Zimmer's scores often get negative feedback regarding his 'power chords' and 'lack of emotion.' Despite this, I found his score to fit nicely with what Nolan was going for in the film. There is a very wide range of genre in the score, providing quiet, intimate moments, and all out action sequences.

All in all, Inception is a movie that proves Hollywood can make money with an original story. The performances bring you in, and the score takes you even deeper. You get immersed in the story and that is what makes this one of my favorite movies. Without a doubt, I would recommend this movie for anyone looking to sit down and have their mind blown.

review: When you think of a dream it is whatever your mind has desired. Inception is based on those dreams you get lost in and do not want to awake from. It is like taking your mind to a fantasy land. If you enjoy adventure, getting stun by dreams, and multi-structured unrealistic thoughts then this is it. The thrill of being consumed by your fantasies is what made me want to see this movie. You should see this movie, because it was sold to people who like action, mystery, and romance. As stated on the website www.IMDb.com, Inception was rated an 8.7 out of 10. Many people liked this movie, because it gave mystery to your mind getting lost in a maze for a moment. His wife Mal (Marion Cotillard) wearing a white flowing dress and a glass champagne, invites him to come out the elevator. He always wanted to experience this in awe moment with her. DiCaprio began to dance with wife and gets lost in the moment of feeling her heartbeat match. It hit him that this moment was not real and steps back from his wife, runs in confusion to the elevator. title: Inception - Movie Review
review:
Inception is a heist film by Christopher Nolan. The movie is based on the philosophical subject called "Dream Argument". The Dream Argument essentially hopes to point out that we cannot distinguish between dreams and reality on the basis of perception. Anything we see, feel or hear might as well be the part of a dream.

The movie takes the Dream Argument to a whole new level by introducing dreams inside dreams inside dreams and more..! It may be said that people inside a dream share a "Dream Space". In the movie, Leonardo DiCaprio's character discovers a way to enter someone's subconscious mind and access his dreams. He uses this to plant ideas into people's minds and also to extract information.

The movie has action and mystery written all over it. It is also food for the mind as it forces the viewers to put their thinking caps. If you are willing to do the needful, this movie should be a treat to watch. In the end it leaves a question which many today try to answer. The film is unique with respect to it's theme and ideology.

title: A complex yet brilliant film for the ages
review:
For many, this film is synonymous with complexity—and rightfully so. Its intricate plot has more than just dreams within dreams but also ideas within ideas. There is more to Inception than just its plot twists, however. Inception is above all the most innovative idea to come out of Hollywood since Donnie Darko but is also an exhibition of fantastic cinematography, good acting, a moving score, and a compelling plot.

There are too many unique elements to dreaming and inception in this story to cover them all, but a list of some of them would include: that five minutes in the real world gives an hour in the dream, the concept of architects who design dreams as mazes, that there are projections of the subconscious who can turn on those who do not belong in the dream, totems, that dreamers use bank vaults as places to hide secure information, the concept of a forger as someone who imitates real people within a dream rather than the conventional definition, etc. Because Inception has so many of these original ideas, all of which are new to the audience, much of the movie must be dedicated to explaining these concepts to the audience. How these ideas are explained and how much time is given to their explanation is critical to the film's success because there is a balance that must be met between providing enough information that the audience can understand what's going on but not so much that the audience is overwhelmed and loses interest in the story. Nolan's execution of this balance is flawless. By using multiple characters to teach the audience (Cobb, Arthur, and Eames) and dividing new concepts up between scenes, Nolan keeps his ideas fresh and manageable for the audience.

"An idea is like a virus: resilient, highly contagious. The smallest seed of an idea can grow. It can grow to define or destroy you." This is how Cobb characterizes an idea and is clearly the definition at work in the film. The audience learns about the process of inception very gradually over the course of the film. We are initially told that it is a means of planting an idea into a dreamer's head and, if successful, making them believe it is their own. Then Eames makes it clear to us that this process is very difficult to master because it requires the most basic stage of the idea in order for it to work. Lastly a much darker piece of inception is introduced: that the idea can destroy the one who receives it. Nolan intentionally leaves out this information until the final confrontation between Cobb and Mal, as it is the key to understanding what happened to Mal and the reason for Cobb's guilt. Part of the Nolan's genius in this film is the way he presents the story of the inception of Fischer and the bargain with Saito to the audience as if it were the main story of the film when really he is distracting us from the real story which is Cobb's relationship with Mal.

A dream within a dream and the concept of inception are the defining characteristics of Inception for most viewers but the real heart of the film is the back story of Cobb and Mal. Throughout the film we are aware that their relationship is significant since Mal works as a multifaceted bridge between the real world, the dream world, and Cobb's memories both for Cobb and for the audience. She is the real antagonist of the film as her character is constantly at work to stop Cobb from succeeding. We see her interference in the dream world from the very beginning of the film where she tells Saito about him and attempts to torture Arthur. She is Cobb's cause of pain in the real world (the reason he cannot go home to his children) and she also haunts his memories' Ariadne discovers Cobb keeps certain memories of her locked away off an elevator in his mind ("These are memories I have to make right" he tells Ariadne.) Part of the genius of this story is that at first the audience is meant to believe that Mal and Cobb's relationship is a vehicle for explaining Cobb's character and the reason he must perform inception on Fischer to be able to go home. But towards the end of the film when Cobb enters Limbo and reveals that he performed inception on Mal which led to her suicide, we begin to realize that it's the other way around; the Inception of Fischer is just the vehicle to explain what Cobb did to Mal and the reason for his guilt. Mal is the basis for the film's theme of questioning the reality we live in and the source of doubt for Cobb and for the audience as to whether Cobb lives in the real world or whether he is still dreaming while his children keep him grounded in the real world.

A film to be watched again and again, Inception is a thought-provoking, mind-bending film for the ages. Its complexity is not limited to its story, but extends to its cinematography, and its score. This film takes special effects, which are sometimes the downfall of a film, and uses it as a strength to build on an already creative script. In today's age of movies where three sequels to Avatar are being made and Hollywood is often criticized for its lack of imagination, Inception is the creativity we've all been searching for.

title: An Action-filled Adventure through each Level
review:
This movie fails to disappoint when it comes to an amazing sci-fi action thriller. Full of action and suspense, this film not only gets your heart racing and blood pumping, but gets your brain working as well, for this movie is not enjoyable unless you understand the concept and science.

Inception is the theory that an Extractor, like Cobb (DiCaprio), can input an idea into the subconscious mind of a subject at dream state. By implementing this idea, one could then control the subject throughout the dream(s) in order to manipulate him/her to reach a desired result, secret, or thought in the end, in hopes to somehow altar reality. In Cobb's case, it's the input of an idea into Fisher's (Murphy) mind in order to somehow bring down his father's multi-million dollar empire, so that Cobb can go home and see his kids again.

FYI: Cobb is a wanted man for espionage and the possible involvement in Mal's death.

The Architect (Page) then builds a series of levels, or dreams within a dream, in order to reach deeper into the subject's subconscious. Due to security purposes, a team member is left behind in each level to look after the others, in case projections, the people in the dream placed by the subject's subconscious, attack. This happens when the extractor rolls off the course of the dream or when the subject realizes they're in a dream.

Every time you enter a new dream, time in the real world slows down in comparison to the dream world, like so:

1 minute in reality is 1 hour in level 1, 1 day in level 2, 1 month in level 3, and so on and so forth.

In order to return to reality, the character must somehow kill themselves. However, if one were to dive too deep into the mind, a "kick" is required for each person in the dream to move back to the previous level.This occurs in sequence until you return to the real world, or else you fall into a state of Limbo, and wander the dream until you find a way out.

Cobb's past is what I feel like the story builds itself on. Unless Cobb learns that the Mal (his wife) he sees in these dreams isn't the real one (cuz she's dead), the whole dream will collapse.

This film is not only an amazing action thriller, but a deep, well- minded psychological drama as well. The characters must think in order to move to the next step, and synchronize their parts at the right time. This thought process is what makes me see not only a man wanting to see his kids again, but a team working together to make it happen, which is why I recommend this movie to you, the reader of this review.

title: Reel Look: Inception
review:
"What do you want?" "Inception. Is it possible?" Written, produced and directed by Christopher Nolan, his 2010 action-drenched summer blockbuster science fiction heist thriller starred a large ensemble cast and, with and official budget of $160 million, went on to gross over $800 million worldwide, becoming the forty-fifth highest grossing film of all time. Nolan's reputation with 'The Dark Knight' helped secure the film's $100 million in advertising expenditure. So is the film as mind-bending as its title implies? Let's take a look.

Shortly after finishing 'Insomnia' (2002), Nolan wrote and eighty- page treatment about "dream stealers" envisioning a horror film inspired by lucid dreaming and presented the idea to Warner Bros. Feeling the need for more experience, he retired the project and instead worked on 'Batman Begins' (2005), 'The Prestige' (2006) and 'The Dark Knight' (2008). Spending half a year on the script, he purchased it from Warner Bros. in February 2009. Filmed in six countries and four continents, it began shooting in June 19, Tokyo 2009 and finished in Canada in November 22, 2009.

The film stars our two leading actors Leonardo DiCaprio as Dominick "Dom" Cobb and Joseph Gordon-Levitt as Arthur, two "extractors", people who perform corporate espionage using an experimental military technology to infiltrate the subconscious of their targets to extract information while experiencing shared dreaming. This skill has made Dom a hot commodity for the world of corporate espionage The target of their latest project is Japanese business man Saito (Ken Wantanabe)caught forever in limbo as an aged man. The extraction is interrupted and the mission failed when sabotaged by a memory of Cobb's deceased wife Mal (Marion Cotillard). Saito reveals that he was actually auditioning the team to perform the difficult act of "inception": planting an idea into someone's subconscious. Their newest target: Robert Fischer (Cillian Murphy), the heir of an ailing competitor Maurice Fischer (Peter Postlethwaite) to break up the break up the energy conglomerate. He wants Cobb to plant the idea in Robert's head of dissolving his father's company. Should Cobb succeed, Saito tells him he will use his influence to clear Cobb of a murder charge, which will allow him to return home to his children. Arthur claims that inception is impossible as it is always possible to trace the origin of an idea. Cobb, claiming past experience, accepts the offer. After setting about assembling the rest of the team, including Eames (Tom Hardy), a conman and identity forger, Yusuf (Dileep Rao), a chemist who concocts a powerful sedative for a stable "dream within a dream", and a graduate student of architecture Ariadne (Ellen Page), (a name taken after the Greek princess mostly associated with mazes and labyrinths) tasked with designing the labyrinth of the dream landscapes recruited with the help of Professor Stephen Miles (Michael Caine), also a mentor and father-in-law to Cobb, they set out to perform the impossible. Though Cobb eventually gets this chance of a lifetime to redeem his life as a thief, a projection of his former wife anticipates Cobb's every move, a projection of which his subconscious created, appearing frequently in dreams/missions as a hostile force.

'Inception' not only falls into the category of a summer popcorn flick but also as a fresh approach of how CGI imagery can be beautifully used to incorporate its way into a story, disregarding showy explosions and alien monsters: objects exploding in slow- motion around a cafe, a city folding in half upon itself, good guys versus villain projections and duking it out amidst the hallway of a zero-gravity hotel. Visually and physically mind-bending in its stimulating high-tech grandeur, this fast-paced blockbuster offers a world where you are never sure where you are nor how you got there and will not let you awake until the film has run its adrenaline- fused course. Until Edith Piaf sings, what is real or unreal, what may be a dream within a dream...within a dream, 'Inception' offers edge-of-the-seat thrills and visual trickery, enlightening the eye and the mind with a bombardment consisting of a slew of special effects and labyrinthian storyline. As long as the top continues to spin, one can hardly want to dismiss the 'kick' when the end credits roll as it cuts to black as the viewer must now "awaken".

title: Inception will make you question what is real and what is a dream
review:
The film Inception (2010) is a cinematic roller coaster that will thrill your imagination and force your sub-conscience to come to the forefront. The picture essentially begins in medias res with Cobb (Leonardo DiCaprio) washed up on a beach in his sub-conscience mind. Then, the story starts over, relying heavily on flashbacks throughout the film to define important aspects of the movie. Cobb is essentially a thief who specializes in extracting information from a person's mind when that person is dreaming. After an incident involving his wife, Cobb is forced to flee and leave his children. Cobb is eventually offered the chance to go home again if he successfully completes one last job; inception. Cobb is asked to plant an idea into the mind of Robert Fischer (Cillian Murphy). Cobb puts together a rather unusual crew of criminals to complete the job. This leads the group to create dreams that mimic the real life of Fischer. This eccentric film is spent jumping back and forth between real life, dreams, dreams within dreams, dreams within dreams within dreams, and so on, until even the audience is questioning what is real.

The theme of the film Inception (2010) is the struggle of finding a balance between what is true and what is not. Cobb delves into the many layers of his sub-conscience in order to relive memories of his past. In doing this, he confuses reality with his dreams. Parts of this concept felt similar to The Matrix (1999), but not enough to feel like a rip- off. It is apparent that Cobb is struggling with problems that are hidden from the audience, but as the movie progresses, the problems become visible. As mentioned previously, Christopher Nolan (the director) relied heavily on flashbacks. With every flashback that follows the previous flashback, more information about the main character, Cobb, is revealed. As I watched this film, I thought that there would be unanswered questions that would leave me either filled with wonder or unsatisfied. But even though the movie does end with a cliff-hanger, the story makes remarkable sense with only one question left to the imagination of the audience.

There were several techniques used in this film in terms of special effects, but a scene definitely worth noting is the anti-gravity scene. During the film's climax, the second layer of the dream becomes weightless. I am not sure why this effect did not carry over into the other layers, but regardless, it was visually stimulating and very impressive.

Another element that is sure to please the imagination of the audience is the motif of dreams. Nobody really knows why we dream. It is a fascinating and confusing concept. The statement that sums up the mystery of dreams best is when Cobb tells Ariadne (Ellen Page) that dreams only seem strange when we wake up. This is one of my favorite references to dreams in the movie.

Overall, Inception (2010) is a deep movie that will leave the audience thinking about what they just saw after they have watched it. The concepts within the movie are creative and fresh. To witness the work resulted from a director tackling an idea like dreaming is a jaw dropping experience. I highly recommend this film to everyone!

title: Artistic, thought-provoking, and original. I can't ask for more.
review:
My number one reason for liking Inception might seem fanboyish, but I'll say it anyway: it's a Christopher Nolan film.

Now, my reasons for liking Nolan's films are too numerous to count, but I'll say this: he is one of the very few directors who makes artistic, thoughtful films on a blockbuster budget. Starting out as an indie director with Memento, Nolan really hit his stride when he inherited the Batman franchise and made his Dark Knight trilogy (which I will cover later in this series). However, he always had a knack for taking original content such as the magician-focused novel The Prestige or creating his own original ideas.

This is where Inception comes in. How many films can you say have been made about the subconscious of the human mind? And how many of those got the budget of Inception? Nolan is ambitious, I'll give him that. Thankfully, he uses his ambition and passion together, making what seems as one pet project after another. His devotion to his craft is rare in today's industry. Inception evidences this beautifully: Nolan wrote his own script and, as is typical for his films, never allowed second unit filming, directing every single shot himself. He is also very particular about his effects, opting for practical, real stunts and visuals instead of generating them on a computer. Inception has less CG shots than even Batman Begins, which is quite obviously mostly real in its effects. This grounds his films in reality and makes them more fun to watch.

Speaking of visuals, let's talk about Inception's aesthetic. Most of Nolan's films are worked on by cinematographer Wally Pfister, and while he has done excellent work in all of his Nolan collaborations, this is his best. The way he changes the color palette through each layer of the dream is quite subtle but very effective, helping us keep track of where we are throughout the complicated climax. Other scenes, particularly in the lowest dream level, show us an excellent knowledge of scale and scope on Pfister's part. The best parts, however, are when he uses high-speed cameras to slow down the film to reflect the time changes between the levels. It ties everything together beautifully and helps us understand how that process works.

That moves us right on to the best aspect of Inception: the story. I can't really go into detail here without spoilers because this is one of the more complex plots I've ever seen. Just know this: repeat viewings are almost required. This is not for comprehension, but rather to pick up on all the nuances that are here. There is so much to this plot that I am still picking up nuances upon watching Inception for the ninth time and enjoying the film even more. In case you can't tell, this is not a movie where you can turn your brain off and slip mindlessly into another world. You have to pay attention or you will lose track of what's happening.

To keep this short, I'll say only one thing about the score and then move on: Hans Zimmer is the best film composer today. This film gave him that title.

Inception's cast is almost as big as I've seen in any film. Leonardo DiCaprio is the top-billed star, but that is incredibly misleading as this film is a true ensemble piece. He also doesn't steal the show in Inception like he usually does, leaving others a lot of room to work. The one thing that is starting to get to me about DiCaprio is that, as good as he is, all of his characters seem the same. They all struggle with their inner demons extensively throughout the course of the film, and Cobb is no different. Outside of DiCaprio, the acting is equally stellar, with Tom Hardy and Cillian Murphy stealing the show. Hardy plays Eames, a forger for Cobb's job who is one of the very few characters with any kind of comic relief. He really shows his range here and proves that he can help carry a film. Murphy plays the subject of the final job, Robert Fischer. I feel that he best embodies how we react to ideas in our subconscious and really made Inception relatable to the audience.

Inception is a masterpiece, and an original one at that, from the man responsible for some of the best films of this century to date. Christopher Nolan really knows how to bring all the elements of a film together into one coherent vision, from the story to the casting to the aesthetic to the score. Every part of this film contributes to the overall vision. Inception is one of my favorite films because it challenges the mind and makes it think. In a world of escapist entertainment, this film makes us explore our minds and our ideas in a way I've never seen before.

title: Wow, What a Brilliant Film
review:
Movies are being made more and more often these days, which means there will be more and more garbage. But it also means we'll get more of this stuff.

Inception is an instant classic! Everything about the film is at least 8/10 worthy.

First of all, the idea. What brilliance! Only a psychological film fanatic like Christopher Nolan could come up with something like this. It's just an incredibly entertaining and mind-blowing concept. (10/10)

The writing is not quite as good as other Nolan films (TDK and Interstellar in mind here) but still keeps our eyes glued to the screen for the whole film. Also the plot/storyline is very interesting, and a bit confusing. (8/10)

The Acting is Near Perfect! Leonardo DiCaprio is by no means my favorite actor. But I will admit he is very talented. And he shines in the starring role. Marion Cotillard, Tom Hardy, Cillian Murphy, and Ken Watanabe all excel in their roles as well. But the person who is most underrated and, in my opinion, gave the best output was Joseph Gordon-Levitt! He is an amazing supporting actor and is really good as the comrade of Dom Cobb. Plus, I dig the name Arthur. (9/10)

The Editing/Music/Visual Effects are insane! The best part about the visuals is that most were done with practical stunts and set pieces rather than CGI or other FX. The classical music background is very soothing in an intense movie. (9/10)

Overall, this film was brilliant and it is my second-favorite Chris Nolan film (besides TDK). (9/10)

title: A mind blowing experience, literally!
review:
It's a brain-twister, believe you me! A daredevilry narrative experiment by writer-director Nolan is every bit as nail biting as it is adhesive.

A hi-tech security consultant (DiCaprio) has devised a contraption that allows him to sneak into people's dreams and extract vital corporate secrets. To complicate matters, his own subconscious is haunted by the figure of his late wife (Cotillard) and their two young children. Moreover, his new mission is fraught with danger as it involves planting an idea in the target's mind instead of merely pilfering one.

Assembling a crack team, the 'dream thief' sends them (and us) down the proverbial rabbit hole where nothing is as it seems.

Needless to say, Inception forever confounds the viewer's expectations. Leaving little doubt as to his talent as a story teller, Nolan demands our undivided attention.

The film is given a further boost not only from Leonardo DiCaprio's persuasive performance but from the imaginative set designs, gravity-defying stunts and a pulse- pounding musical score by Hans Zimmer.

Inception is recommended whole-heartedly for those who love skittish encounters.

DiCaprio plays a professional thief who commits corporate espionage by infiltrating the subconscious of his targets. He is offered a chance of redemption as payment for a task considered to be impossible: "inception", the implantation of another person's idea into a target's subconscious.

title: Nolan's best film
review:
Christopher Nolan is currently one of the most-hyped directors around: I don't quite follow as bland characterisation and formulaic tension seem to be consistent hallmarks of his films, as well as a lack of an identifiable artistic vision, but perhaps this is what translates best to a mainstream worldwide audience.

His work is certainly 'good', vastly superior to the blockbusting likes of Michael Bay, so maybe I should cut him some slack.

Inception is a fantastic movie experience: original special effects & set-pieces are what it's all about here. There's at least two "WOW" moments (the first time the streets 'flip', and the action around the slow-mo car crash). The story itself is forgettable, along with the afore-mentioned characterisation issues (Levitt is decent, tho'), but the ideas are interesting and these are translated well by the production.

The experience doesn't stay with you once the film is over...there's not much interest in a repeat viewing either. But it deserves its 8/10 for being entertaining (and for Di Caprio being watchable for a change).

Now Cobb is being offered a chance at redemption. One last job could give him his life back but only if he can accomplish the impossible-inception.
