title: Inception is just about Perfection!
review:
Inception is probably the most original film since The Matrix back in 1999. I think one of the key components that will either invigorate audiences or turn them off is the fact that it's not based on an already established name, be it an adaptation or a sequel. That in itself is refreshing enough but the genius conceit of Inception is that it believes so much in the world it's created that it leaves very little catching up time for the audience. The rules for Extraction and Inception are laid down thick and fast and woe betide the fellow that insists on a pee break. Miss even two minutes of this film and you're lost.

But in laying down the rules, the second half of the film (in which DiCaprio's team implement the Inception heist) acts them out with aplomb. We have dreams within dreams within dreams and things that happen in one plain of reality directly effect that in the next, for example: whilst the team is unconscious in freefall in one, in the subsequent dream they're all weightless, and whilst a van in which the team is asleep tumbles down a hill, the gravity in the next starts to shift (giving us that awesome corridor fight from the trailer).

Christopher Nolan really has taken everything he's learned from making mature adult blockbusters and utilised it here with maximum effect. To say it's thinking man's blockbuster is understating things but, unlike the Michael Bay's of this world, he does not feel the need to treat his audience like kids. Whilst Inception may hold a 12A certificate, that's not to say it's for children of that age, not because of any of its content I must add, just that the plot, which is perfectly written and executed, will just be too much for those that crave robots hitting each other.

But, that said, there is a lot here that will appeal to that demographic. The visuals, whether it is during much of the trippy dream imagery or the outstanding action sequences, are spectacular. Whilst grounding much of the dream world in reality, that's not to stop Paris from folding in on itself or have gravity shifting from wall to wall.

But, as stated, what makes Inception work is it stubbornness to stick to it's established rules. So ten hours in real time equates to a week in the dream world but a dream within that dream equates to six months and a dream within that dream equates to ten years and so on, so whilst moments that are instantaneous in one dream, the team knows that they'll have around twenty minutes to get things done in the next, etc. Once you get your head around it, you have to marvel at how well the filmmakers have been able to juggle the different time frames within the dream world. It pays off in spade and once everything comes together in the end.

title: Exceptional, but flawed
review:
Inception is often criticized for being not quite as deep or intelligent as it tries to be. I disagree, but think that it is hugely flawed in two ways:

1. It tries to be an action movie, but the action doesn't work. Why does it try to be an action movie?

a. because obviously, action movies draw audiences

b. because Nolan seems to believe that the highest achievement in movie-making would be to turn the action genre into something deep and meaningful

2. It is overly long and many portions of it are just boring and not entertaining at all

In depths: While the Mombasa chase sequence was somehow acceptable considering the moment it occurred and its rather low importance, serious doubt came up with the Level-1 shoot-outs; nothing here ever felt really threatening, and the almost exclusive use of real-world submachine guns felt totally out of place. But the snow fortress was an insult. The action was lifeless and unintendedly (of course) comical. Did Nolan actually believe shooting good action here? In fact, the sequence was cocky in the sense that Nolan seemed to believe that even the most trivial, anachronistic action would, in the context of this ingenious movie and helped by some magic notes courtesy of Hans Zimmer, somehow blossom into something cool... whatever that would be. But unfortunately, he overestimates himself and his collaborators here and at the same time underestimates the audience as well as the current status quo and the rich universe of action cinema culture as a whole.

With 148 minutes, Inception runs way too long, and considering the altogether failed action pieces, this is where a strong and confident editor would have been much welcomed. However, the problem goes deeper into the structuring and the actual writing of the film, as simply cutting away the action would complicate the obvious intention to make us experience everything as happening simultaneously. In other words: A lot of the action is just filler so we have something we can cross-cut to. Take this away and we have a problem. A problem with the weighty concept of synchronicity. The only real solution here is rewriting. So, after all, tinkering with the screenplay for 10 years might still haven't been enough, so finally, Nolan made an unripe movie.

A couple more negative aspects of the film: Most of the cast feels out of place and gives presence to the fourth wall. Gordon-Levitt looks very generic and pimped up, and somehow his casting never pays off. His face is so clean and smooth that you're actually waiting for something deep to happen with or because of him... but there isn't anything. He doesn't really do anything in the movie, he's a mere squire. Tom Hardy, with his confidence and physical impressiveness, faces a similar pitfall, since as long as nothing deep happens to or because of him, he feels like a guy waiting for his shot on a lead role, again somewhat damaging the fourth wall. Michael Caine and Ken Watanabe are not only totally wasted in this movie, but every single time he's in the frame, Caine's dressing and hairdo bring up one question: Where is Batman?

It seems quite obvious that Nolan deliberately chose to make every character but Cobb explicitly one- dimensional. Whatever meaning this implies (dream or reality; what is mainplot, what is subplot etc.) or function is strengthens, it could have been achieved by casting much less known actors thereby leaving the fourth wall more intact, pulling us more into the story and at the same time maybe giving an interesting new face a chance on the silver screen.

Now the positive: Inception is one of those movies that can make you think about it for a long time after seeing it. It has a unique atmosphere, a very strong mood and a masterpiece score. The score, in fact, has been haunting me for days and gets some heavy rotation on my home stereo. DiCaprio and Murphy turn in great performances and are a joy to watch. Effects and CGI are done to a very high standard and are woven into the story well.

6 out of 10 stars. If the movie was overall as bad as the action sequences, it would be 1 star. If the action was as good as the overall film, it would be 9 or 10 stars. Everything as-is, it's somewhere in the middle, since the awful fighting scenes, especially in the snow fortress setting, really taint this movie. However, my overall feeling is rather positive, so it's 6 stars at the end.

The strength of the movie, what will stick with you, is its themes. Dreaming, reality, non-reality, guilt, ideas, originality, obsession, forgetting, forgiveness. If this sounds exciting to you, chances are you will like Inception.

title: The film held my interest, kept me in suspense, and made me question whether or not it would be possible for extraction or inception to occur.
review:
The 2010 science fiction film "Inception" was written, co-produced, and directed by Christopher Nolan. "Inception" has large ensemble cast, including Leonardo DiCaprio as Dominick "Dom" Cobb, the extractor. He is a professional thief specializing in stealing secrets by infiltrating the dreams of his victims. Ken Watanabe stars as Mr. Satio. He is a Japanese businessman who hires Cobb and his team for a very specific job. Joseph Gordon-Levitt stars as Arthur one of the members of Cobb's team. Ellen Page, who I loved in "Juno", stars as Ariadne the newest member of Cobb's team. Marion Cotillard plays Mal. Mal is Dom Cobb's deceased wife. Cillian Murphy stars as Robert Michael Fischer, Jr. He is the only heir to a business empire, and Cobb's next target, the victim that Mr. Satio has hired Cobb to infiltrate. The cast includes several additional members including Michael Caine, from "The Cider House Rules", as Professor Stephen Miles, Cobb's father-in-law. The story centers on Mr. Satio's desire to have Cobb and his team infiltrate the mind of Robert Michael Fischer, Jr. through a level of dreams to plant an idea in his subconscious, the act of inception. Cobb must except this job, and complete the task at hand, if he hopes to be reunited with his children. The story takes many twists and turns throughout the film.

The theme of the story is the idea that people can share a dream. Not only can a dream be shared, but information can be extracted from one individual's mind by another individual, through a dream. This idea is taken a step further by suggesting that in addition to extracting information; it is also possible for one individual to plant an idea into the subconscious mind of another individual. This film explores the reality of such a process, as well as, the dangers involved in performing the act. The film addresses the serious ramifications of such a manipulation. If I were to relate "Inception" to another film of the same genre, I would choose "The Matrix". In "The Matrix" the mind is also manipulated. The method may not be the same, but dangers to the mind certainly exist in both films.

Many scenes were shot in slow motion to allow the viewer to follow the action. This technique was used to stretch the moment and intensify the effectiveness of the scene. In some scenes, the use of slow motion exaggerated the actors' movements. The viewer is then able to see the exhaustion or frustration of the characters, while they try to accomplish certain tasks. Sound was often used to intensify the transition from one scene to another. At various times throughout the film, sound was used to build suspense or set the tone. The film began with intense music. I could feel the suspense building.

Although I am not a big fan of science fiction films, I felt that "Inception" was well made. I thought that Leonardo DiCaprio was outstanding in this film. He was believable as Dom Cobb. The film held my interest, kept me in suspense, and made me question whether or not it would be possible for extraction or inception to occur.

title: Dreams feel real while we're in them. It's only when we wake up that we realize something was actually strange
review:
Directed by Christopher Nolan

Starring Leonardo DiCaprio, Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Ellen Page

Written by Christopher Nolan

'A skilled extractor is offered a chance to regain his old life as payment for a task considered to be impossible.'

After the Dark Knight arrived, Christopher Nolan has earned my respect. Inception was coming out 2 years afterwards and I wasn't going to let myself miss an experience from such a talented storyteller of film.

What can I say that hasn't already been said about this terrific film? This is a film that you could get lost in. Not in the way that it's hard to follow the story but a way that you don't want it to end. Christopher Nolan creates a world that everybody dreams of. A 'superhuman' universe in a way that you could do anything you want, in any way shape or form. His writing is at a complex apex in this picture. There is so much information delivered throughout, sometimes you feel like you won't be able to keep up. But rather than just explaining through words, he lets you see with your own eyes exactly what his brilliant mind was trying to illustrate in this film. This film has one of the best beginnings I've seen. Everything is presented to you; the story, the characters, the information, the jobs, the creativity, the imagination and the motives of why certain characters do what they do. It's only later in the film that all these aspects go deeper and deeper into the story. Christopher Nolan used a little more special effects for this style of storytelling than his others in the past but it isn't overwhelming. It's at a point where it's necessary and doesn't intrude what's happening in the frame.

The acting in this picture actually complemented the story itself. It's hard to find decent actors for such a complex and wonderful story but they did wonderfully. Leonardo DiCaprio is brilliant as always. He excels in representing characters with a dark past and problems they need to confront. Cillian Murphy also does an amazing job and I'm surprised that not much praise was given to him from critics. In the dramatic scenes are where Murphy really stands out from his peers and colleagues. Great skills. Ellen Page's character really annoyed me the first time viewing this film in a way that she can't keep her nose out of other people's business. But I realized that Ellen Page's character is the audience in this picture. Whatever she sees for the first time, the audience sees as well. It's as if we are Page's character wanting to figure out why certain things exist and why DiCaprio's character has such a dark past. Clever Mr.Nolan.

There's not much to be said about the music/score in this film. Hans Zimmer and Christopher Nolan really see eye to eye on how the music plays a part in the storytelling. Upbeat races and long continuous bass beats really satisfy you throughout the film. These two can't fail.

Inception is a very complex and new story. Many people won't catch the magic with only one viewing but if you commit yourself to watching it again and again, you will notice something different every time. It's beautifully orchestrated and one of the best films of 2010.

title: A Near Perfect Film
review:
In this film, they advertise that Leonardo DiCaprio is in it, because he's a very famous actor. Across the top of the poster, it says his name. He is #1 at the top of the Top Billed Cast of 'Inception'. Now, if you look up Leonardo DiCaprio, his very top movie, at #1, of his Known For list, there is 'Inception'.

We have never seen anything like what is in this movie. It is a complicated, smart, action-packed drama/action film directed by Christopher Nolan, director of the 'Dark Knight' trilogy. I have no idea how the writers of this movie came up with such a masterpiece. The story of this is that DiCaprio's character, who is able to extract people's dreams, has a job that will get him from France (where he is now) to America, and back to kids, but he's not even sure this job is possible. It is to perform inception on a future owner of a very larger company.

When this movie starts out, you have no idea at all what is going on. You do eventually find out, though. I was extremely confused and was nearly doubting this film because I had no idea what was going on. When you do find out what was going on, your mind clicks into the movie. I thought that the film showed us what was going on at the perfect time. It didn't wait too long for us to loose interest, and it didn't happen too quick so that there was a boring part. Basically the whole movie was very interesting to me.

This film takes a challenge on itself to dig deeper and deeper to show us viewers everything about what's going on leading up to the huge, intense, action-packed sequence at the end of the movie. I shouldn't really say the end, because it starts a little earlier than I thought it would. That's one of the few problems in this movie. I thought the huge group of scenes started a little too early because I thought it could have taken more time to build it up. Anyway, it prevailed at the challenge it took, and there were many very cool things that happened. Scene by scene it takes us deeper into the planning of when they try inception. It gets very complicated there, but not really for us, like it was in the beginning. I meant it got complicating for the characters, kind of. They have to come up with a huge plan for the inception part of the movie, and you don't really have to completely invest your brain into it, because you're about to see it happen. Well, at least I didn't invest my brain into it.

The beginning was pretty action-packed, and the build-up was very interesting, but those parts of the movie are nothing compared to the last part of the movie. It's almost like they're sections: Section 1: Beginning; Section 2: Buildup; Section 3: Inception Part. The longest section was the Inception Part. I think it was about an hour and a half long, and for almost that last hour of the movie, I was at the edge of my seat. It was so intense, and I was going for the characters so much, I was basically talking to them, event though they couldn't hear. That's not weird, but seriously, I was saying, "NO! NO! Don't do it! Come on, come on!!!" There was so much action and there were many, many cool parts having to deal with the dreams. They were even cooler than the cool parts in the Buildup. By the end of the movie, you're so invested into the movie, you're not thinking about anything else. That section was so incredibly awesome to me. 'Inception' just truly amazed me. There was very good action and writing, the two things that prone to going bad the most in a movie.

So anyway, the ending was excellent, too, just like the rest of the movie. Especially the very last scene before the credits. It was just... Awesome. I really thought they couldn't have done that any better. I'll stop talking about it now. Well, I will buy 'Inception' on Blu-Ray. It is an overall excellent movie. It's two and a half hours long, but it justifies itself as a long movie. There were almost no boring parts in this movie. I actually think it would be worse if it wasn't this long. I strongly recommend this movie.

title: Indebted to inception
review: Inception -thought would be a okay movie from mr.pitt but it swirled me around... In a summer of remakes, reboots and sequels comes "Inception," easily the most original movie idea in ages. Now "original" doesn't mean its chases, cliffhangers, shoot-outs, skullduggery and last-minute rescues. Movies have trafficked in those things forever. What's new here is how writer-director Christopher Nolan repackages all this with a science-fiction concept that allows his characters to chase and shoot across multiple levels of reality. This is, in some ways, a con-game movie, only the action takes place entirely within the characters' minds while they dream. Following up on such ingenious and intriguing films as "The Dark Knight" and "Memento," Nolan has outdone himself. "Inception" puts him not only at the top of the heap of sci-fi all-stars, but it also should put this Warner Bros. release near or at the top of the summer movies. It's very hard to see how a film that plays so winningly to so many demographics would not be a worldwide hit. Not that the film doesn't have its antecedents. "Dreamscape" (1984) featured a man who could enter and manipulate dreams, and, of course, in "The Matrix" (1999) human beings and machines battled on various reality levels created by artificial intelligence. In "Inception," Nolan imagines a new kind of corporate espionage wherein a thief enters a person's brain during the dream state to steal ideas. This is done by an entire team of "extractors" who design the architecture of the dreams, forge identities within the dream and even pharmacologically help several people to share these dreams. Leonardo DiCaprio plays Dom Cobb, a master extractor, who is for what initially are vague reasons on the run and cannot return home to his children in the States. Then along comes a powerful businessman, Saito (Ken Watanabe), who offers Dom his life back -- if he'll perform a special job. Saito wants Dom to do the impossible: Instead of stealing an idea, he wants Dom to plant one, an idea that will cause the mark, Robert Fischer (Cillian Murphy), to break up his father's multibillion-dollar corporation for "emotional" reasons. Meanwhile, you meet the other team members -- Arthur (Joseph Gordon- Levitt), Dom's longtime point man; Eames (Tom Hardy), the forger; Yusuf (Dileep Rao), the chemist; and Dom's father-in-law (Michael Caine), who is not on the team but the professor who taught Dom to share dreams. Dom's late wife, Mal (Marion Cotillard), haunts his own dreamworld like a kind of Mata Hari, intent on messing with his mind if not staking a claim to his very life. He doesn't let on about this, but Dom's new architect, Ariadne (Ellen Page), figures it out -- which makes her realize how dangerous it is to share dreams with Dom. A good deal of the first hour is spent, essentially, selling the audience on this sci-fi idea. As you witness an extraction that fails and then Dom's recruitment of his new team around the world, the movie lays out all the hows, whys, whos and what-the-hells behind "extractions." If you don't follow all this, join the club. It will perhaps take multiple viewings of these multiple dream states to extract all the logic and regulations. (At least that's what the filmmakers hope.) Something else might come more easily on subsequent viewings: With incredibly tense situations suspended across so many dreams within dreams, all that restless energy might induce a kind of reverse stress in audiences, producing not quite tedium, but you may want to shout, "C'mon, let's get on with it." This is especially true when the hectic action in one dream, a van rolling down a hill with its dreamers aboard, causes a hotel corridor to roll in another, producing a weightless state in the characters. Even Fred Astaire didn't dance on the ceiling as much as these guys do. Probably what "sells" this tricky movie is the actors. In his second consecutive movie to question reality -- "Shutter Island" came earlier this year, remember -- DiCaprio anchors the film with a performance that is low-key yet intense despite hysterical chaos breaking out all around him. Page too displays sharp intelligence and determination in the face of this absolute jumble of reality. Especially surprising is Murphy as the mark; you find yourself genuinely sympathetic to a guy who just wanted to catch a little shut-eye and finds his mind kidnapped. It also is nice that Nolan strives to keep CG effects to a minimum and do as many stunts in-camera as possible. This photo-realism certainly helps to keep the dream realities looking more plausible. Credit cinematographer Wally Pfister with so neatly blending the real and surreal without any hokey moments. Ditto that for production designer Guy Hendrix Dyas and the various stunt coordinators and effects teams. Meanwhile, editor Lee Smith does a Herculean job of juggling those different realities. Sometimes originality comes at a cost though: At the end, you may find yourself utterly exhausted.

title: World Class Masterpiece
review:
A masterpiece. That's one thing you have to know before watching this film. Few films even come close into the amount of sheer spectacle that this film have. Great plot, great acting, and great cinematography. The movie is brilliant from the start and it will no doubt confuses your mind until the twist come, and all the plot-holes is answered. No spoilers, but Inception will still leaves you wanting more long after its end credits.

Probably the greatest thing that Inception have amongst other films of its kind is the plot itself. A heist inside a person's mind. However how silly the plot can get, the film will make you believe that it is possible, and it never out steps out of its boundaries for it too become too complicated. Don't get me wrong, the movie is complicated and will leave some viewers scratching their heads after it ended. Even after you watch it over and over again, there will be some scenes that you still can't understand. But the movie never pushes itself to the point where it finally becomes unwatchable.

The other great thing that this movie have is the brilliant acting. Leonardo Dicaprio steals the spotlight with his role as Dom Cobb, the world-class thief that agrees to do one last job that could get them home to his children. You will drawn in by his character and feel the same emotion that he's feeling. Happy, angry, sad, you will feel every emotion that he's feeling. And in my opinion this is his best acting so far. The other casts are great too and each plays their role brilliantly. One such role is Arthur, a former thief like Dom which is played excellently by Joseph Gordon-Levitt.

The last applaud should go to the cinematography, and with it, the director himself. Christopher Nolan is brilliant and it is a disappointment that he didn't get at least nominated for best director for Oscars. From the opening sequence of the film until the ending, Inception is like a roller coaster ride but one that stills open rooms for emotional scenes. Congratulations, Nolan. You don't have to have an Oscar when you have the world's respect.

title: to dream or not to dream
review: Inception is a film produced in 2010. The film is about Dominic Cobb and his road to recovery of almost everything he lost. Inception is set in the distant future, where they have developed a machine to enter someone's subconscious or their dreams. Dominic is one of the first persons to use this technique. After the suicide of his wife, Cobb found out a few things about dreams. Namely, people could lose their mind while invading dreams because they are unsure whether they are dreaming or awake, and secrets can be extracted from dreams. Cobb uses the knowledge he has on dreams to create a criminal organisation that enters the dreams of people to steal secrets and because of this and the strange suicide of his wife, he becomes a wanted criminal. While doing one of their schemes, it backfires and they are found out. Mr Saito, the man who captures Cob and Arthur (one of Cobb's friends that help him with stealing the ideas from the dreams), has a proposition for him. He asks him to plant an idea in someone's head instead of stealing it. Cobb wants to turn it down but he is offered a reward he can't turn down: his criminal status would be removed so he would be able to go home again and see his kids. Obviously this summary hasn't spoiled the end yet and hopefully it made you curious to find out the rest of the story. Inception is a science fiction thriller with quite some action. Even if you do not like thrillers, Inception still has a great plot, some amazing stunts and special effects that you wouldn't want to miss. The first great thing about this film would be the plot line. The plot is amazing; you are really drawn into the story of Cob and his impossible quest. The plot is not one straight line; it twists and turns like a river, especially when you watch the film for the second time. The first time you watch Inception, it is just a great film with some very cool action thrown in. The second time you watch it you will notice interesting details that you had missed out the first time and will make you rethink everything that happened. Those details make the film very realistic and you will start thinking about the whole concept of dreams. What do you dream about? Are there really secrets hidden in our subconscious? And how could you control your dreams? Another thing that makes this film amazing would be the special effects. Those special effects are very important because most of the time in the film was spent inside different dreams in different people. Everybody dreams, so you will know that in your dreams anything could happen. You dream of impossible things, and everybody has different dreams. That is exactly why special effects are so important in Inception. It explains why the film could only be produced this recent. Ten years ago, we did not have the knowledge and techniques yet to do justice to the dream world. Nowadays, a lot more can be made with CGI (computer generated imagery) and Nolan used it for quite a bit of shots, but not for everything. Where other directors would use a green screen, Nolan would try to do most of the things with stunts and a real dÃ©cor. For example, there was this fighting scene in a hallway that was rotating. Nolan created a real rotating hallway and made the actor play the scene while the hallway really was turning. The actor commented that he was very glad that Nolan made him do this: not only was it a lot of fun to do it, but it was a lot more realistic than just hanging him on a contraption and tell him to act like he was off-balance. Others would just put the actors in front of a green screen and let them play their parts, but not Nolan. He is convinced that doing real stunts without a dream screen is a lot better than a green screen, and does the most extreme things to realize these. There is just one small drawback on Inception, which is that it is a very long film. The film is more than two hours long. That is quite some time to stay concentrated on one thing, especially if it is as complicated as this film. If you have a small attention span while watching it and you miss some information, it is quite a challenge to get what is going on during the rest of the movie. That said, it really is the only drawback. Of course there is always the pause button, or you could of just rewind parts of the film. But then again, because it's so difficult, you concentrate intensely on the film and most don't even notice that it's so long. All in all Inception was a great film even though it was very long. The special effect and stunt were very convincing especially the ones that took place inside the dreams. The combination of the two was superb. Add the plot and you have the best thriller of the year. Or, Inception combined so many plot elements that one could consider it to be a drama, or an action, and it even contained comical elements. Leonardo diCaprio, Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Ellen Page, Ken Watanabe, Marion Cotillard and Michael Caine form a very impressive cast. Inception is a film that nearly everyone would like, except for people who watch films to relax. Cobb's story will hunt you for a long time, both in your dreams and normal life.

title: Positive review of "Inception"
review:
"Inception" Will Captivate Your Mind

I have just seen the movie "Inception" by Christopher Nolan, an English director and writer, and I would like to make my opinion about this incredible piece of art. This movie was released in 2011 and has been a success since the begging. "Inception" can be seen as an action, adventure, and mystery movie. It is filled with intrigue and it will break your mind. If I had to rate this movie, I would give it a 9.9 out of 10 because it very well done and the topic of was very interesting. It is not a surprise that "Inception" won 4 Oscars and another 33 wins and 109 nominations. It can even be considered as the best movie of this decade.

"Inception" talks about Cobb, Arthur, Ariadne, Eames, and Saiko who adventures into the mind of Robert Fisher with their skills of extraction to implant an idea into him. Cobb joins the group together and they prepare themselves for the hard task of making their first inception. They wanted to implant the idea that Fishers father wanted him to start over his life when he died and that he should not continue his company. They were doing this because Saiko, the rival company owner wanted Fisher's company out so that he could be the leader of the market and he hired the team to perfume the mission. Cobb accepted this because Saiko promised that he would clear his history so that he could return to his children because he had conflicts in the past that didn't allow him to see them. They enter into fisher's mind and find out that his subconscious have been trained against threats like the one they were tying to create. This makes the journey harder. In order to be able to actually insert an idea, they had to go very deep into the dream. They end up having to be dreaming in a dream of a dream so that they could be as deep in Fisher's subconscious as they could.

First of all I would like to comment about the actors performance in this movie. Leonardo Di Caprio who played as Cobb in the film did, in my opinion, an extraordinary job. I actually felt as if all the conflicts and problems he faced were real and also he made me feel as if his history with his wife was a reality. Di Caprio can be considered as one of the best actors in actuality because of his performance in movies like "Titanic "and this movie can be seen as one of his best works. Joseph Gordon-Levitt who played as Arthur, as well as Di Caprio, exited the expectations in this movie. He as well never seemed fake with his actions and was able to become the character completely. Ellen Page, in my opinion was the worst actress in the film. She made an incredible performance, maybe even one of her best, but still I could notice the lack of experience she had while been compared with the other actors in the movie. I believe that the action movies aren't her strength and she should maybe get involved more in other genres.

One aspect that I could exalt about this movie was its special effects. One scene that stranded out to me was when Cobbs was teaching Ariadne about dreams and how she was going to be the architect of them. She then decided to alter the laws of physics and bended the city so that the roofs of one build would be touching the roofs of another building. Also, another scene that was very interesting was when Cobb explained about the world that he created with his wife because of the incredible architecture. Also, the movie had a very good script because it described a lot of aspects that the audience needed to know to fully understand the movie because of the confusing concepts such as of inception, extraction and limbo. Also, a very interesting aspect f the movie is the fact that Christopher Noland decided to leave an open ending, which has created confusion to many. I believe that this technique fitted perfectly in this movie because it made people to think about the movie even when it had ended.

Two very important lessons that I learned from this movie are that you are never alone in life. This was taught to me because even though Cobbs had his internal conflicts with his children and his wife, Ariadne constantly asked him to let her in so that she could help him and she did. Also, that everything has a root cause. I learned this because the plan of the mission was to put in a simple idea that would grow in Fisher's subconscious and would change his life. In life, people always ask why bad things happen to them but if they look closely to the reasons that lead to what happened to them, they will always have the fault.

The writer of this critique is Alejandro Carranza he is a student in Lincoln School from Costa Rica. He is currently in ninth grade. He is doing this film critic of "Inception" because he saw the movie in the class of Film Appreciation of the professor Pablo Morales and was asked by him to choose one movie to criticize. Alejandro enjoys watching movies in his free time. His favorite sport is soccer and he has been playing this sport all his life.

title: A postmodernist movie to be 'digested', not to be merely seen!
review: First things First: It appears so that when we are talking about criticisms or critic, we are not talking about evaluation, rather, we are doing "critique" and NOT criticizing the text (text here means any genre in which a story is narrated - here, it is narrated via the medium of Cinematography - a film). So it appears that some of the reviews written here have the sense of criticizing as if evaluating or judging it based on what their personal taste in this particular movie was. Furthermore, criticizing a movie needs an unbiased eye - since some reviews written here have strongly recommended the movie or found it so astonishing based on starring actors/actresses, director, music composer, etc! But from what we know of a really "objective" kind of criticism, it must not look up for exterior factors (exterior factors are any those factors, other than what is seen in the movie!) So I think any criticism should ONLY be limited to the work itself being criticized! Now I would like to invite you to the following review. 1. Characters/persons/Postmodernism: Here it is needed to heed on what we mean by character! Do NOT mistakenly take it as person! Person refers to real human beings but character is not attributed to actors of the movie, they also refer to objects or things! I would like to say that the 'dream' being introduced as the motif in this movie is a strong character; we could also say that the dream itself is so characteristic in the life (or plot) of the people that we see in the story being said in the movie! OR even so characteristic about us - real human beings - out of the movie & in real world! isn't it?! Dreams as even Freud once said and its interpretations are indeed of high value! But let us focus on the movie.. I seems like the movie is a complete "postmodernist" movie! From what we know about postmodernist novels or even movies, the text does not follow a logical time line or sequencing of the events and that is clearly seen in the 3 layered dream displayed in the movie! More, postmodernist movies do not emphasize the reality of objects or even the world around us.. To be more exact, postmodernist genre does not force us to believe what is 'real' around us; instead, it tries to blur the distinct territory of reality with that of a dream or any other imaginary or parallel worlds. "Postmodernism" tries to enforce a kind of chaos, a mixture of cinematographic elements in this sense to create a radical understanding of an old concept and to embody it into a new shape! Here in this movie, 'dream' is presented into OUR world, so naked, so bizarre and so REALISTIC that induces a certain kind of doubt about the very world we are now existing on! We would then ask ourselves: "what if THIS world is NOT real and we SHOULD wake up from this tiring dream?!?!" Certainly you remember the scene at the hotel when Cobb's wife (=Mal) attempts suicide! There you go! She thought that now, this world is not what she wanted! She still NEEDS a dream! but Why?! According to what Freud says about dream-work in the field of psychology, and his classification about 'id', 'ego' and 'superego', due to some restrictions in REAL world, or better say due to sociocultural barriers, the repressed emotions and feelings (or real desires of mankind or what our 'id' really wants us to do or to have) are trapped in our 'unconsciousness'.. so what is its significance? Those yearnings are resurfaced in a dream, where no barrier or no restriction exists! It's a total freedom in our 'unconsciousness' where you are free to do anything or to have anything you want! (It makes sense, huh?) So, when you dream, you think like you can have ANYTHING or ANYBODY beyond limits! Mal also believed that in her dreams. Another feature of postmodernist works is that they intend to create a chaos deliberately! They hold the agenda that we are living in the world of chaos where nothing and absolutely nothing follows a schedule or a definite plan... Everything is internalized: our true feelings too. They focus on 'intertextuality' and complexity of different texts or discourses! In Ariadne's dream where she creates vertical-shape buildings which later turns on itself creating an all-in-all (360 degree) world where no sky exists and instead, the ceiling of their dream is another layer of structures and buildings!! It even amazes Cobb! Somewhere else, I would emphasize that postmodernist movies tend to portray the lack of coherence, consistency or unity that what we definitely expect our universe to possess! 2. Totem/dream & life/gaps: I have to ask you this: "what does a totem mean in this movie?" Of course I think it's an icon, a motif being portrayed numerously during the movie and you know that a repetition is a very important element not only in movies but also in novels or any other sort of genre.. We all know why they used their own PRIVATE totem... they just wanted to realize or better say get sure that they are NOT within a dream!!! (what an irony! isn't it?! we are living in a world and still we need to do something to make sure we are not dead! we are still living, not imagining or pretending to live!!!) But another question is why Cobb lets go of his totem on the table at the end, and runs after his children?! It would be simple! If you remember, he refuses to look at his children when he is AWARE that he is in a dream...but finally, when he makes sure no threat comes from Mal anymore and when he returns home, he does NOT bother to wait for the totem...! instead, he focuses on his REAL totems in his life! = His CHILDREN!!! Thanks. Bahram Kabiri

title: Inception, Illusion and Reality

title: dream and reality
review:

It more looks like a parallel dimension with a little different physical laws than a dream world with no rational (rational in the sense of coherent) rules at all. In that aspect David Lynch is the true master of dream world.

Inception can also be seen as a doom scenario that shows the colonization of one of the last remnants of "no man's land" in our civilization, the dream world. What once used to be a battleground of our unconscious drives and desires becomes a battleground of energy corporations. But than again, maybe today our energy corporations are in fact embodiment of our unconscious drives and desires? After all if in the above sentence we bracket "corporation" we will get just "energy", which in a way is just another word for drive or desire.

title: great.
review:
At heart a heist film, however only a director with such a strong and grandeur vision could capsulate the mechanics of a heist film and present an innovative, complex, ambiguous and original approach to this genre while still providing the epic concepts associated with blockbuster films.

Inception follows the story of Cobb, a man who specializes in the concepts of mind theft, however Cobb latest job requires 'inception', the method of planting a idea in someones mind.

The opening sequence of inception establishes, quite evidently, the brilliant concepts of where this film succeeds, from brilliant editing, masterful soundtrack, amazing set pieces while being interwoven with an innovative substance. All these concepts lead to a brilliant creation of a dream premise, which is presented as being quite complicated, however the film creates a balance between this complicated plot and also, in a sense, it's simplicity, which allows a story that is quite easily to follow.

Like most Nolan films, 'Inception consist' of some breathtaking set pieces. The reason why the set pieces are amazing is due to the fact that they are authentic. Rather than use CGI (besides one scene) Nolan incorporates his set pieces as real settings, which is astonishing, considering the example of one set piece which consist of a fight sequence in a revolving hallway. Furthermore the story has an emotional backbone in relation to the Cobb and his wife, who is downright scary!

As i noted before, the editing in this film is masterful and deserving of the Oscar. For instance, the last 40 minutes consist of four simultaneous action sequences which one would think has the potential to lose viewers in it's own momentum, however it does not, due to the fact of the film's brilliance in the editing compartment. Furthermore Hans zimmer once again provides a grandeur score, each sequence is heightened greatly in the spectacle department simply due to the music, from the opening sequence of 'the dream is collapsing' to the ending with the poignant 'time'.

The brilliance of this film is that it constructs a great parallel balance between the intellectual and spectacle, as the film provides complex concepts which mentally engage the viewer while also providing the action spectacle. The only criticism is that the film relies on it's complex ideas to conceal plot holes, nevertheless 'Inception' most definitely compensates these flaws from it's sheer ambition.

A very satisfying film that deserves appreciation.

title: A consummate director shares his dreams--literally
review:
Inception is about as complex a movie that Christopher Nolan will ever make, so far. It is clear evidence in this cinematic entrepreneur's vast mind that film making and dreaming can conjoin on mutual grounds and become a total thrill to the audience and a box office success for Hollywood. The film, which is a genius creation ten years in the making, uses the concept of dreaming on an epic scale. There's a taste of Kubrick's The Killing in there, a few artistic designs likened from Akira Kurosawa no doubt—but the psychology of it all is entirely Christopher Nolan. It is, after all, an idea from his mind.

The facetious thing about the film's plot is how it makes a metaphor for everything sacred to dreaming. In this movie, the verbal exchange, "I'm sharing my dream with you" does not elicit a whimsical date on a beach but actually sharing tangible dreams. Nolan's movie is in control of its own universe. The rules, regulations and taboos of his dream lore are explained, sometimes too thoroughly, in an interconnected fabrication of quick cut, edited scenes that all heighten into a climatic ending. For pleasing the audiences, as well as giving a little more taste to their mindless popcorn munching, the film succeeds. Others, like film pseudo-intellectuals, might criticize the absence of ambiguity. Is it because Nolan has thoroughly mastered his own world? Or that his tedium reached new levels of egoism? Whatever the answer, it sure as hell warrants the viewer to think about these things. Yes. Thinking after a movie can still exist through the throngs of visually evocative extravaganzas. (And for the record, Nolan's movie does have the power to evoke—thought in this case).

With the world set up, and as long as audiences are invested enough to follow, the plot unravels as professional dream extractors arrange to plant an idea in the mind of a company rival. Their operation unfolds like a heist as they delve deeper and deeper into the target's mind. This is all good fun, and probably one of the best McGuffin's in years. The actual grit of the story comes from Dom Cobb (Leo DiCaprio) who is guilt stricken over planting an idea in his wife's head which lead her to her suicide. In a psychological battle reminiscent of Nolan's other movie Memento, Inception's protagonist has all the workings of the quintessential Nolan character. By following Cobb, we not only suffer his psychological breakdowns, but we understand that there is indeed a human element behind the extraneous plot. As a result, we empathize, sharing both Cobb's dreams and his realities.

For a first time viewing, Inception will certainly excite. By the last shot, it incites multiple viewings—not just for clarity, but for another grasp of Nolan's intricate perspective on dreaming. I have seen it four times now. The action and thrills remain, but the premise—the very idea of the film—is still an intrigue. In the long line of movie makers, Nolan has accomplished the remarkable—he's shared his dream with us. Literally.

title: Inception - Don't Read if you haven't Seen the Movie
review:
In this movie Leonardo DiCaprio plays Cobb a man desperately wanting to go home to the US but cannot because of a previous incident that occurred. He is not an ordinary man, though he is a man that has knowledge of how to enter into people's dreams. This knowledge that he has causes Saito (Ken Watanabe) to seek him out for a job that would be dangerous however the reward was great. Saito wanted Cobb and his team , Arthur (Joseph Gorden-Levitt), Eames (Tom Hardy), Ariadne (Ellen Page) and Yusuf (Dileep Rao) to plant a thought into Robert Fischer's (Cillian Murphy) mind who was a wealthy man that could enter into business agreements that could have a significant impact on the worlds business market.

The theme of the movie is guilt as Cobb tries desperately to forgive himself for a mistake that he made and as he tries to get back home to his children that are currently out of his reach. The motif of the film was very clear in that the dominant idea was inception. Planting of an idea or thought into someone else's mind. Therefore the name itself clearly defines the movie as the central idea.

Likewise, the movie was shot using inside/out editing. It did this by beginning with unfamiliar scenes or caused the audience to ask questions then it helped you to understand. For instance at the beginning of the movie how Cobb is brought into a room with a very old man (Saito) is how it starts, however you are confused as to why the movie starts there only to understand how both Cobb and Saito both came to be there later in the film. They used the same technique in reference to Mal (Cobb's wife). She is deceased yet you don't know what happened or why she continues to show up in Cobb's dreams until he explains it to Ariadne while they are in a warehouse in Fischer's dream.

This movie was definitely different in content however it reminds me of the Matrix. The reason being is because both used extremely sophisticated technology, both took place in the future and both had settings that constantly bounced around from one place to next. I believed the movie to be a good one, especially if you are a science fiction lover. The movie however can be a little complex for those of us that don't like to live in the clouds. Honestly, this is a movie that you will definitely have to watch more than once to have a clear understanding of the events.

title: A great action flick, but pounds the eye, ears and brain a bit with a sledgehammer
review:
I thoroughly enjoyed this elegant puzzle-film / hard-driving action flick but thought how much more it might have been.

It takes on the complexities of the dream world in a way that mirrors the MATRIX, or TRON, an alternate-world film where the laws of physics can be bent, and the same people can play many different roles.

The fact that one person is killed every minute or so, and occasionally more, in the midst of crashing, explosions, beatings and other mayhem actually interferes with the ability for the observer to enjoy the story and care about the characters. This isn't a gentle ride, this isn't a roller coaster. This is a beating. And so it's every man and woman for themselves - especially the audience.

There is no time for us to care about the characters, except the protagonist, because, oops, the walls are crashing down and three people are shooting at us!

The dream world also is multi-layered, but Nolan's layers are not subtly tied to each other, just as the cast's relationships do not exist apart from the single story layer.

For example, every layer looks real and very similar. The entire movie is about dreams, but there is only one surreal element in them : the juxtaposition of buildings. In true dreams many things that could not exist including people, personalities, decisions, even time-lines, are molded, twisted and amalgamated in remarkable and unreal ways.

It would have been a better use of the opportunity to explore those layers rather than making them just different sets in the same James-Bond like world filled with testosterone and adrenaline.

Where old houses are mixed with the modern, it simply doesn't work. The beloved house from youth just looks like a heap. The characters who created those places loved them, and they could have been shown with greater love.

What might have been? Characters that are mostly from one dreamer but infected by the sentiments of another, one world slipping into another world altogether - Paris and China mixed up on the same street.

What might have been? The story elements themselves reflect emotions. The walls are made of feeling, and when they are threatened they fall, but often they are loving us, protecting us, encouraging us. When we fall in love with that world, it falls in love with us and we fall deeper and deeper into the dream. And yet that dream at ever deeper levels, tells us more directly about what is truly inside us. Yes, even the dreamworld would be warning us about the dangers.

The film buys shock and confusion but pays with lost character, story and sentiment.

Dreams can be confusing and shocking, and in this way the story certainly is dreamlike.

In Dom's testimony at the end to his wife he says she is not really as deep and multi-layered as his real wife. Well, that applies to every character in the film except Dom.

What might have been? The most multi-faceted and interesting of characters and relationships in the dream world, not the "real" one.

That would also have helped us understand the sentiment at the end, about coming to peace within one's own self, and finding a richness within, love within our own selves that may indeed be the real source of our happiness,the hidden reality that informs the dream world we live in during our waking lives.

And indeed, Dom's inner Mal might be much more subtly in-tuned to Dom than any flashback of her. Dom's Mal is not just memories, as the film suggests. Characters in dreams can be as fully fleshed out as we are because they have the full resources of the subconscious, which "awake" people do not. They can be much funnier, wiser, stronger and helpful than we are.

And if Dom realized that the woman who killed herself was not really the woman he loved, but a stranger with an obsession he could not save her from, a woman who loved her dream more than her husband or children; and that the woman he really loved, who was really caring and filled with self-sacrifice was a part of himself, his own projection, that might have helped him let go.

That "inner" Mal might explain that Dom made a tragic mistake and to forgive himself as he forgave the real Mal her obsession. That inner Mal would remind Dom that he did indeed spend a lifetime together in that second region with the real Mal, and that somehow she got lost, addicted, unable to get out of the honeymoon, unwilling to do so. He failed to save her,but she was already lost before he planted the doubt in her mind. She didn't want to leave that dream world anyway, and so doubt was the only hope for her escape, though it failed.

The story Nolan crafted was brilliant, but he did not bring it fully to life.

In the absence of that depth, we are just left with a man who accidentally caused his wife's death and who cannot really escape, except into fantasy. How much more this film might have been!

And then the audience might have walked away with a deeper insight: Each of us only knows the other by the image we make of that other person, and that image, fed by our senses and the other's behavior, is the only way we can know them in this dream world in which we live.

title: Stunning!
review:
Blew me away actually, very original (-planting an idea in someone's subconscious while they sleep) takes place, and tries to get the absolute most out of the story, action and graphics within the rules it created for itself for this inception to take place.

Even though I found the movie very entertaining, in the end I felt it left me hanging. This was because the movie kept telling me over and over again how brilliant it was, and how superbly complex it was, while in fact, it wasn't complex at all. The basic story is very simple actually. It's just made complex with a lot of gimmicks.

This isn't really a bad thing, all movies do it. So I wondered whether 'feeling conned' is a good argument. I guess it mainly had to do with the ending of the movie. The ending is a cheap way to have your audience question whether it was real or not. Of course, there is no correct answer. And that's OK. But why ask the question than? If it all wás real in end, the movie is that much better. Now they choose to be oh so 'deep' and 'thoughtful'. Where yet again, it really is not.

I guess the 'feeling conned' sentiment comes from all the 'this movie is oh so complex, oh so deep, oh so thoughtful' gestures it makes. But it fails to deliver actual arguments (for me at least)to back that claim up. The gimmicks are (needlessly) complex indeed, the basic story itself is not, not by a long shot.

This all sounds very negative, and the movie doesn't deserve it, it's a very good movie and to all the people I know I recommended watching it. Mainly because it spawned interesting conversations. However, that bitter after-taste of 'feeling conned' has made me come to feel this is a movie without heart. To me it seems they didn't want to make this movie so 'complex' and 'deep' because they loved doing so or because the story deserved it. They only did it to try and trick me to think this was a brilliant movie. And when you try to do that with me, I tend to back away.

title: Dream-thievers
review:
I actually didn't "get" some of Christopher Nolan's previous movies, like "Identity" or "The Prestige" and so was wary of the hype surrounding this blockbuster of his. I'm glad to say that I finally got it this time as this is a spectacular sci-fi thriller with more levels than the Empire State Building, demanding, but rewarding the viewer's full attention throughout.

It really impresses in every way possible, the imagination which fires the story, the lucidity with which it's complexity is brought to the screen, the pacing which is relentless throughout, but never wearing and the circular resolution of the story by the end sequence.

Yes there are holes in the plot, (like how did Fischer come to be ready for the team's attempt to hijack his memory?) plus the motivation for the elaborateness of the team's plan doesn't convince as it should, but this is an instance of "trust the teller, not the tale" as, futurist elements part, it rattles along, fuelled by Hans Zimmer's pounding background music.

The acting is uniformly good, Di Caprio leading his assorted "dream-busters" with aplomb, the acting by all executed with razor-sharp timing and conviction, which the story demands. The cinematography and C-Gen SFX are eye-popping, particularly Cobb's first dream-walk with Ariadne, the weightless fight-scene, the train's appearance in city centre traffic and much much more.

This film unquestionably is Nolan's best and raises the bar for tech-thrillers in the modern age.

It's one dream you won't want to end.

title: The Dream is Real.
review:
The Dream is Real.

Dom Cobb is a thief. In fact, he's the best in the business. But he specializes in a new form of theft unlike anything before it; extraction. Dom steals peoples secrets, hidden deep in their subconscious, by infiltrating their dreams. His rare skill has opened the door to a lucrative, but dangerous, career in corporate espionage. But now he finds himself unable to return to his home country, the United States, for fear of arrest and prosecution on false charges of murder.

However, Dom has been given a second chance. A new job offer presents the possibility of having the charges disappear so that he may return to his country and his children. The catch is that he must carry out a nearly impossible extraction deep within the subconscious of a powerful corporate tycoon. He has a shot at redemption, but only if he can finish the job and make it out alive.

Inception is an intricate, complex, and fascinating movie with killer effects and cinematography. A sci-fi thriller with lots of action and a bit of mystery and drama to boot. It also has a good cast which includes Leonardo DiCaprio, Joseph Gordon-Leavitt, Ellen Page, Cillian Murphy, and Pete Postlethwaite amongst others. Viewers are coming to expect a lot when Christopher Nolan releases a film, but he keeps on delivering.

I think that's worthy of a big hats-off to the film makers and its been a while since i saw a film that had such a great closing. Excellent watch and one of the best films in the last 10 years.

title: A Visually Stunning Intellectual Coup!
review:
Inception, as writer-director Christopher Nolan's intricately executed conceptual coup, deals with the fractured reality of dreams, and the consequences of what could be described as mind-control warfare. In this film, it is clear that Nolan is freed from any need to satisfy formulaic convention, which is part of what makes it so exciting to watch. He seems to masterfully blend intense and inventive action sequences with emotion – something that is rarely done in films that rely heavily upon physical gymnastics.

Leonardo DiCaprio's "Cobb" is a corporate raider who is tasked with infiltrating the minds of other men, with the intent to steal their ideas. The world marketplace as we have known it, is filled with individuals who have been doing just that for centuries – only not exactly through any obvious form of mind control. The Microsoft and Apple story is a perfect example of modern-day corporate thievery, when you think about how Bill Gates managed to take the existing Windows concept, apply it to another software business and ultimately copy it away from Steve Jobs and the Apple team.

Cobb is hired by a powerful billionaire to do the opposite of what he has been doing: to implant an idea into the mind of a rival, so that the rival believes it is his own concept. This ideology, in and of itself, could be considered a groundbreaking aspect of the story line. The motivation for Cobb to take on the project, is as an irresistible way for him to return to his family, from a forced exile.

The state of Limbo, which only contains things each character has built themselves, might explain why Cobb's limbo depicts so few projections. It would be far too easy to assume that Cobb remains in his "limbo" world, simply because we are never really shown where anything started. Instead, it would seem more logical that he would ultimately return to his children. Throughout the film, in so many frames, we are shown that they are the most important people to him.

This film is as much about how information is used to control situations and people, as it is about a man who has developed a way to do it through dreams. When Cobb expresses his distress that he used his own wife in a mind-game experimentation, it is easy to see why this would cause conflict for him. Because if you have any level of ethics or morals, doing this type of thing, without someone's knowledge and consent, would be one of the worst betrayals you could ever perpetrate upon another human being. What could be worse than causing someone to make disastrous decisions (as in committing suicide) because they believe it is necessary in order to get back to reality? In studies of sociopaths, manipulating information is one of the classic ways that they gain control over people. And that is what makes them so dangerous.

One of the most brilliant aspects of this film is the fact that an ambiguity remains. We are shown in the film that each person's totem is uniquely theirs, and that merely touching someone else's totem makes it invalid. So how could it be that Cobb, who is using his deceased wife's totem, would have any sort of access to its power? Cobb's connection to his wife's totem could be seen as another way that he has attempted to control her. Especially once he admits that he first experimented with the inception program on her.

Cobb's children do not age throughout the film, and they seem to match his exact memory of them. It would make sense that this memory surely would be out of date since he'd been away from them for so many months. When he finally does see their faces, they look exactly as he envisioned them, but, according to the film's costume designer, are wearing different clothes. Even so, shouldn't his children be older than in his memories? But what if time stopped at that moment. This would allow him to resume his life as he knew it. Which is exactly what human beings do when their dreams have ended.

When that totem top is spinning at the end, it seems that Cobb has dismissed it. He's not looking at it, because he doesn't care. Could it be that since he realized how he tried to control his wife (whose totem that was) – he therefore realizes that it is pointless to try to use it any more? What matters most to him at this point, and probably always, is his children. Anyone who has had children understands this connection. Ever having to leave young children before they are fully developed is a great fear of many parents. There is a huge responsibility to caring for people that you bring into this world.

Also, in the film's opening moments, we see Cobb's hand, with a wedding ring. Noticeably, he seems to only wear the ring when he is in the dream world. By the film's end, he is no longer wearing the ring. This seems to confirm that the top eventually stops spinning and that Cobb returns to the real world.

There is great potential to get confused and lost in this film, just as there is in life. In essence, many people learn that there are many realities to believe in. One person's reality is often not someone else's. Life is, a great deal of the time, about interpretation. What means a lot to one person, may mean nothing to someone else. Forcing your reality on anyone almost never comes to any good. We either learn to accept and tolerate that others have different realities, or we struggle to control them into ours. That's one of the great conflicts of life, and this writer believes, one of the main points of this brilliantly executed, luxuriously entertaining and mind-bending films.

title: Challenging Our Cinematic Sensibilities
review:
Inception proves the point that a Hollywood film can move beyond mere entertainment and challenge the viewer to wonder "what the f*#^ is this all about?" One can't argue that the cinematic medium makes passive audiences of us all. Countless movies – comedies, dramas, westerns – you name it, we viewers plop into our seats, chomp popcorn while the action unfolds and carries us to the rolling credits, snapping us out of our trance. Christopher Nolan's tour-de-force isn't your usual heist film. Sure, some of the elements are there – an international group of thieves, the Job, and a ticking clock deadline. After that, it's a whole different type of film altogether. Described as a "sci-fi heist thriller", Inception demands a lot more than blink-blink, chomp-chomp. The drive-by summary is: The Job - Cracking into a grieving energy mogul's (Robert Fischer, played by Cillian Murphy) unconscious mind to plant an idea.

The Thieves - Led by guilt-ridden Dom Cobb (DiCaprio), the Team swells to include point man Arthur (Joseph Gordon-Levitt), architect Ariadne (Ellen Page), chemist Yusuf (Dileep Rao), forger Eames (Tom Hardy), and mega-rich client Saito (Ken Watanabe). They must share a drug-induced dream down three levels, something that hasn't been done. Each member of the team – except Saito and the sleeping Fischer – carries a totem, a special item that reminds them they're in a dreaming state.

The Ticking Clock Deadline – Extraction, the act of removing ideas from someone's mind, is the standard practice among the world of corporate espionage that Cobb inhabits. This two-level process requires the Architect to build a complex world of mazes that the team can move about in freely, as the team descends deeper into the levels of shared dreaming. The Chemist provides the powerful sedatives as the Point Man keeps track of the "kicks" meant to move closer to the waking state. A Forger can replicate into someone else, for the purpose of misleading the potential victim. Inception – the job that Mr. Saito is paying for – requires the team to enter a third level, which is considered a risky and unstable realm to control.

Are you still with me? What moves Inception beyond the Sci-Fi heist genre is the underlying dramatic obstacle that threatens to engulf Cobb into a permanent fourth level of sustained madness, along with his late wife, Mal (Marion Cotillard) – and puts the entire team into harm's way. One aspect of this "dream-within-a-dream" environment is that injury can occur, which awakens the participants, but death is the "risky factor" in a third level. Cobb – on the run after being blamed for Mal's death - agrees to the job after Saito promises to clear his name, so he can return home to his waiting children as a free man.

The puzzle for Cobb is that he uses his free time to enter a fourth level of dream state because it seems more real than his life without Mal. When is he awake? Is it when he's dreaming? Cobb's subconscious longings and obsessive day-dreaming allows Mal to freely wander into the job, as a seductive wild card that endangers the entire assignment at every level. Ariadne's task is compounded as Cobb looks to her for guidance to sort through the complex network of sorrow and desperation, while seeking to bring the job to a successful conclusion.

This reviewer loves this film so much, simply because Inception dares the audience to fully consider this multi-dimensional experience. The only drawbacks are the casting of Marion Cotillard as Mal and Leonardo DiCaprio's occasional over-acting. Ms. Cotillard's constant refrain of "you promised" begins to detract from her otherwise adequate performance after the third time. It wouldn't grate on our nerves if she had varied her delivery just a bit. As for DiCaprio – after almost 22 years of experience he still has a problem with key scenes that demand intense emotion. Hanging out of a window, melodramatically screaming "Oh my God, no!" leaves one wondering why this otherwise gifted actor can't move beyond such overblown histrionics.

It took nine years of film experience and research for Christopher Nolan (The Dark Knight, Memento, The Prestige) to bring his ideas about lucid dreaming to life as Inception. The film takes place across England, France, Tokyo, Tangiers, Los Angeles, and Canada, as the Team races to the heart-hammering finish. Nolan's film boasts a flawless musical score, countless special effects and elaborate sets, not to mention a script that demands the viewer see the film at least twice to truly relish this unique cinematic creation. While such ho-hum movies like The Social Network may scoop up awards this year, rest assured that Inception will be viewed, imitated, and written about for decades to come.

title: A Dream within a Dream
review:
Christopher Nolan, who I believe embodies the neo-noir genre beautifully, departs from his characteristic style in this one-of-a-kind epic. This surreal narrative is incredibly involving, inviting the audience in without them even realizing the complexity of the plot. Nonetheless, after it seems that the film's different "layers" pile upon each other, they are perfectly brought to a poignant close, for Cobb and Fischer especially. The audience can only emerge from the cinema questioning reality itself.

As far as the acting goes, DiCaprio performs his best role as Cobb, who essentially is in an emotional close-up throughout the film. Overall, the cast could not be better - and they all deserve recognition, but DiCaprio stands out as extraordinarily admirable.

The Productions Team deserves the most applause for this production, for so many of the films fantastic effects that bring the subconscious and surreal into existence on screen, and before the camera. I was most impressed to learn that very little of the featured special effects in the film, such as the flooding castle or the exploding café, were generated by computers. Even down to the Free-Fall Hotel and rotating corridor, all of it was constructed, which gives the film a creepily realistic appearance, while creating the impossible - which is what Inception is all about.

This, in my opinion, is Nolan's greatest work, in complexity, scale, and overall satisfaction. He cuts no corners, and the whole is many times greater than the sum of its parts could possibly be. Inception will always rank as one of my favorite films.

title: #1 on my list
review: Christopher Nolan has written and directed a masterpiece for the ages. I have created my top ten best movies ever seen list and this is standing proudly at number one. I have heard the arguments against this film and they normally consist of viewers that were confused, couldn't get invested in the storyline and thought that the characters didn't get any backgrounds for us to get fully invested in them. Here is how I see it, and by no means do I condemn those that dislike this film. I tend to look at these characters as people involved in an Ocean's Eleven type plot. We don't get to know the background of everybody, but they all have specific talents that are needed for this job. Keep in mind that this movie is not really a character piece even though we do focus on Cobb for the entire film. In my personal professional opinion, the plot isn't confusing, just layered. For those that actually pay attention to the plot of a film, this movie has a very strong pot that is beautifully orchestrated throughout the 2h 30min run time. One only need to look and listen for what is going on. If you are one to fall asleep during a film longer than 2h then skip this until your wide awake. This movie does take a few watches to understand the gravity of everything going on and it only means your human if you finish the film and ask what the f**k just happened. The action is so well shot and is mind blowing to watch all the SFX. Now I wish to address the end all and be all of the reviews. The end shot of the movie. Many people have speculated as to how to decipher the end of this movie. I have heard the argument that it was all a dream. His kids were the same age so he must be in the dream world and not reality, and then there is the argument that I personally believe in and have the easiest time swallowing which is that he finished the job, got home and he is safe and sound in the real world. My answer may be completely wrong or I could be right on all cylinders. I honestly don't care what the real answer is because for all we know Chris Nolan made that ending intentionally to make us believe all these things and never agree on one answer. Whether or not there is a definite answer I am unclear about. Nolan loves secrets. The reason I find my answer easier to believe is because I have watched this movie four times (so far) and that seems to be the most logical answer and the one I am satisfied in believing. If somebody came up to me and said that I was wrong and they knew the real answer I wouldn't say prove it, I would say, OK, but this is what I believe. This movie is my favorite because I think about this movie every day of my life and recall that beautiful shot of the city folding and the hotel fight scene. All memorable. Now to end my review of this movie, I will address a question that everyone asks and nobody seems to know the answer to. People constantly ask why there is a snowy James Bond movie set in the climax scene. People say it is unnecessary and doesn't make sense. If you think back to when Ariadne was recruited, she was the brains behind designing the levels of the dream. So basically, using his creative mind and without telling us, Nolan wrote that Ariadne's character designed this level purely from her mind. He takes a liberty with this because it can by anything. We never hear or see Ariadne directly saying to the audience that the final battle will be in this setting, but she's just created it from her mind. Nothing is wrong with this, it just adds a grander and more dramatic scale. Maybe Nolan is a big Bond fan and wanted a set reminiscent of this. Nothing wrong with that. Nolan has crafted the most wholly original screenplay I have ever seen unfold onto the screen. While his ideas were influenced by other films the story itself and how it unfolds has never been done before. I doubt that I will encounter a movie better than this anytime soon, but it is possible. Until then I invite everyone to watch this film and bask in glory that is Inception.
